gap_scenes.title: The Letter Unfolded Again
gap_scenes.text:
She read it a third time before the candle guttered.

The letter had arrived at Colorno in the afternoon, carried upstairs by a footman who could not have known what he held — a folded sheet from Vienna, from a woman Isabelle had never met, written in French with a lightness that made the words seem almost careless. Almost. Isabelle had pressed the paper flat against her writing table and traced the signature with one finger: Marie-Christine.

Now the July evening lay warm and close around her. The windows stood open to the park, and the smell of cut grass came in with the insects. Isabelle put the letter down and looked at the dark ceiling.

She had written back, she knew, too eagerly. She had told Marie-Christine that her feelings were too strong for eloquence, and this was true and also embarrassing — she was nineteen, she was about to be transported like goods to a court she had never seen, to marry a man she had never met, and the only person who had written to her from that place was a princess she did not know, and already Isabelle loved her.

She picked up the letter again. The victory over the Prussians was in there too, General Laudon, the news that had made her beside herself with joy. She was a good Austrian, she had said. She would be. It was simply the truth.

But the other thing — the line about showing her the joy of being able to tell her things — that was not about Prussians at all. That was something else.

She folded the letter, creased it precisely, and set it inside her prayer book, which was the only private place she had.

gap_scenes.title: Counting the Germans in Parma
gap_scenes.text:
By August, they were arriving in small numbers — aides, chamberlains, an Austrian lady-in-waiting with broad shoulders and a Viennese accent — and Isabelle stood at the upstairs window of the Palazzo del Giardino and watched them cross the courtyard below as though they were birds of a migrating flock that had come for her.

Five more weeks. She had written it to Marie-Christine and the number hung in the air of every room.

She tried to imagine what the woman looked like. From the letters she knew the handwriting — urgent, curving slightly to the right — and she knew the tone: generous, a little teasing, warm in a way that pressed close against the formal address. She knew that Marie-Christine played the harpsichord, and that she had written about victories, and that she thought Isabelle's qualities did not deserve such feeling as she'd offered.

On this last point Isabelle disagreed violently and in silence.

She had been drawing in the afternoons to pass the time. Bad portraits, mostly, of people she could not quite remember. She thought perhaps she was trying to draw faces she had not yet seen. She crumpled one attempt and threw it toward the basket and missed.

Her maid came in to say that two more German gentlemen had arrived below.

Isabelle pressed her forehead against the warm glass of the window. Five weeks. The summer smelled of thyme and dust, of the dry Italian earth that had been her home for all her years, and she was leaving it, and she was not sad. She was something she had no word for yet.

gap_scenes.title: First Sight at Schönbrunn
gap_scenes.text:
The ceremony lasted two hours and Isabelle did not see her clearly until it was nearly over.

There had been the procession, the presentations, the Empress watching everything with that particular attention that felt like being measured for a cabinet. There had been Joseph, her husband, standing beside her with a careful courtesy that she was already learning to read as neither warmth nor coldness but simply the way he held himself in public. There had been dozens of faces, all turned toward her, all performing welcome.

And then, at the edge of the room, near the tall windows that looked out over the formal garden, Marie-Christine.

She was not what Isabelle had constructed from the letters. She was more immediate than that — shorter, with an expression that moved quickly across her face, watching Isabelle across all the intervening silk and ceremony with something that was entirely unguarded. When their eyes met, Marie-Christine smiled. Not the court smile, which Isabelle was already learning to recognize as a kind of mask. The other kind.

Isabelle felt the recognition strike her somewhere below the ribs.

Later, when the presentations had concluded and the groups had rearranged into smaller conversations, they were brought together formally, and Marie-Christine took both her hands and said something quick and warm and a little wry about the journey from Parma, and Isabelle laughed — a real laugh, surprised out of her — and thought: so this is the voice behind the letters.

She had been in Vienna for less than a day and she already knew that the next years would be organized around a single gravitational point.

gap_scenes.title: The Harpsichord Lesson
gap_scenes.text:
The room was too warm for October and the harpsichord stood near the window with the lid raised, and Marie-Christine sat at the bench with her back to the door, playing a passage over and over that she could not quite resolve to her satisfaction.

Isabelle had been standing in the doorway for a full minute before Marie-Christine noticed her.

She stopped playing. She did not turn around immediately. There was a pause — the kind that holds more information than words — and then she turned, and her expression was the one that Isabelle was beginning to catalogue: the one that looked a little embarrassed to be caught in something genuine.

"You heard that," Marie-Christine said.

"I heard all of it," Isabelle said. She came further into the room and stood beside the harpsichord, looking at the keys. "You were doing this part —" she indicated a cluster of notes "— differently each time."

"I know which part."

"It was lovely each time."

Marie-Christine gave her a look that contained several things at once, and Isabelle met it without flinching. This was something she was also learning: how to hold Marie-Christine's gaze. It required a particular courage, not because the gaze was unkind, but because it was so entirely direct.

"I'll let you see the music," Marie-Christine said, "when it's ready."

"I'll hold you to that," Isabelle said, and sat down beside her on the bench without being invited, and after a moment Marie-Christine began to play again, and neither of them moved apart.

gap_scenes.title: Saint-Etienne
gap_scenes.text:
There was always somewhere to be.

Isabelle had understood this about court life within the first week — that one was always already late for something, always just completing something else, always visible in the process of arriving or departing. Privacy was not an absence; it was a skill, practiced in doorways and in the intervals between obligations.

On the day she had to go to Saint-Etienne, she had spent the whole morning aware that Marie-Christine was somewhere in the other wing of the palace. Not near. Not reachable by any ordinary means. It was a peculiar kind of ache, knowing the precise direction of someone and being unable to move toward them.

The carriage rattled over cobblestones. Isabelle sat very straight and looked out the window at the November streets of Vienna, the early dark already collecting in the alleyways, the breath of horses visible in the cold air. She was thinking about a different morning, one she had not had, one in which there had been no Saint-Etienne and no obligation and she had simply gone upstairs.

She thought: this is already a pattern. The wanting and the going somewhere else. The letter she would write afterward describing only the absence, not the wanting.

She was in a mood like a dog. She recognized this about herself without approval.

By the time she returned it was dark, and the palace windows were lit from within, and she thought she could see, on the upper floor, the room where Marie-Christine would be, and she went upstairs as quickly as dignity allowed.

gap_scenes.title: Court Mechanics
gap_scenes.text:
There was a version of court life that was machinery, and a version that was theater, and sometimes Isabelle could not tell them apart.

The Archduke — her husband — moved through both with a kind of mechanical precision she had come to find almost soothing in its predictability. He was not unkind. He was not particularly present. This was the arrangement, and Isabelle had understood it very quickly, and had filed it away without resentment.

What occupied her more was the question of what Marie-Christine had said to him, or he to her, or what had passed between them on some afternoon she had not witnessed. Marie-Christine had an influence over him that she wielded lightly and rarely — Isabelle had seen it once or twice, a word placed at the right moment, a redirection so smooth it barely registered. She had been impressed and also unsettled, not by the power itself but by how little Marie-Christine seemed to value it.

"If he knew everything he owes you," Isabelle wanted to say, and did not say, because there were always people nearby.

Instead she watched. She was good at watching. In Italy she had developed a whole inner life built on observation, and Vienna was simply a richer subject.

She watched Marie-Christine move across the reception room, exchanging words, touching an arm here, laughing there, and felt the familiar compression in her chest that she had not found a name for yet, or rather had named, and then decided the name was too large to be safe.

gap_scenes.title: St. Nicholas Eve
gap_scenes.text:
The Feast of St. Nicholas fell on a December evening when the palace smelled of beeswax and fir branches brought in from somewhere cold and far.

Isabelle had her own small suite of rooms by then, and she had begun to know which footsteps outside her door meant what. She knew the Empress's ladies by sound. She knew the particular quiet that meant Marie-Christine was passing in the corridor rather than approaching.

On St. Nicholas Eve, the Empress Maria Theresa sent Isabelle a small gift — a token, formal but warm — and wrote to thank her for something, though Isabelle was not entirely certain for what. She sat with the Empress's note for a long time, feeling the slight unreality of being thanked by the woman who had summoned her from Parma like a piece of necessary furniture, and who had turned out to be something far more complicated.

She wrote to Marie-Christine: please tell me if you admitted to Her Majesty that I was informed of your treason.

"Treason" was their word for small conspiracies of the friendly kind. It made Isabelle smile even writing it. It was the kind of word that only worked between two people who trusted each other with the irony — who understood that the mock-severity was a form of intimacy, not a form of accusation.

She sealed the letter and looked at the guttering candle for a long time before she called the footman.

Outside, the first snow of the season had begun, and Vienna was going white and quiet, and she was nineteen, and she was in the right place.

gap_scenes.title: The Curling Animals
gap_scenes.text:
There was a whole taxonomy of minor irritations that Marie-Christine could produce, and among them — Isabelle had discovered — the worst was the business with the heated tongs.

It was not the curling itself. Isabelle could tolerate a great deal in the service of appearance. It was the way Marie-Christine stood over the operation with an air of proprietorial interest in the outcome, as though Isabelle's hair were something she had a stake in, which she probably did, and this was exactly what was intolerable about it.

"You are," Isabelle said, sitting very still while the maid worked and Marie-Christine watched from the chair by the window, "the most unbearable creature in this palace."

Marie-Christine looked pleased with this assessment. "That seems unlikely, given the competition."

"In matters of hair. Specifically."

"I only want it to look right."

"It is already right."

"It will be more right."

Isabelle met her eyes in the mirror and held the gaze for a moment longer than was strictly necessary, and then looked away because looking away was sometimes the only way to prevent something else from happening in a room with another person present.

The maid finished. Marie-Christine came to look and tilted her head with the expression of someone who has won, and said nothing, which was the most maddening possible response.

Isabelle thought: I would write her a letter about this. I would say, with all possible gentleness, that she is unbearable. She would find it funny. I would mean it, and also not mean it at all.

gap_scenes.title: Grace and Gratitude
gap_scenes.text:
She had woken at six to a body that was not entirely her own.

This was the new condition — the nausea that arrived before full consciousness, the heaviness in the chest, the way her body seemed to be reorganizing itself around an agenda she had not set. She had sat up carefully and waited for the worst of it to pass, and then written to the Empress to thank her for a grace she had been granted — some arrangement, some permission, some small adjustment to the machinery of duty that Maria Theresa had quietly managed on her behalf.

Gratitude was one of the currencies of this world. Isabelle had grown up understanding this, and she was good at it — not false gratitude, which she found intolerable to produce, but genuine acknowledgment of kindness received. The Empress had been kinder than she'd expected. It complicated things.

She had slept a little better the previous night. This also complicated things, because she had been almost used to lying awake and using the time to think about Marie-Christine.

It was a habit she could not seem to break, and was not certain she wanted to. In the dark at three in the morning, with the whole palace sleeping around her and Joseph breathing quietly in the adjacent room, she would think about the afternoon she had spent in Marie-Christine's apartment, the way the light fell across the table, the particular sound of her laugh when something surprised her.

She finished the letter to the Empress and tried to go back to sleep and could not, and lay looking at the ceiling instead, which was at least familiar.

gap_scenes.title: The Pearl Necklace
gap_scenes.text:
There were eighteen days left until her birthday.

Isabelle was not accustomed to counting down to her own birthday. It had never seemed worth the trouble. But this year was different — she was turning nineteen on December thirty-first, and the thirty-first of December was also the last night of a year that had contained everything, and Marie-Christine had mentioned something yesterday about the pearls, and about dinner, and about wishing to speak to her, and Isabelle had said yes to all of it without knowing precisely what she was agreeing to.

The pearls were in a small box that lived in the top drawer of her writing table. She opened the drawer now and looked at them without taking them out. They were nothing extraordinary — a shorter strand, pale gray-white, the sort of thing one lent to a sister for an occasion and then received back later, or perhaps did not receive back, and this too was a kind of intimacy.

She closed the drawer.

She thought about the conversation Marie-Christine had promised her. She thought about all the things that could be said in a conversation that could not be said in a letter, or in a corridor, or in a room with three ladies and a footman and the Empress's portrait watching from the wall.

The December light was failing by half past three. Isabelle lit the candle herself, without calling anyone, and sat in the small brightness of it and thought about the new year coming, and the girl she would be on the other side of it.

gap_scenes.title: The Last Hour of the Year
gap_scenes.text:
At midnight the bells of Vienna rang and Isabelle stood at the window of her apartment and listened.

She had turned nineteen at some point earlier in the day — the birthday was officially December thirty-first and the palace had acknowledged it with the correct formalities — and now the year was ending, and she felt the precise quality of strangeness that came from being at a threshold, looking in both directions at once.

She had seen Marie-Christine at dinner. They had sat too far apart for anything but the ordinary exchange of glances across a table, which was its own form of conversation, one she had grown fluent in over these past months. A look that said: I see you. A look that said: I know what you are thinking. A look that said: there is too much silk between us and I am choosing not to think about that.

Now the dining room was empty and the candles were being extinguished by invisible hands all through the palace, and the bells were ringing, and Marie-Christine was somewhere in the east wing, and she was nineteen years old as of today, and she had been in Vienna for three months, and everything had changed.

She pressed her fingers against the cold glass of the window. Outside, Vienna was alive with sound — people in the streets, carriages, the celebratory noise of the city welcoming something new.

She thought: I will write to her tomorrow. Good evening, good new year, I love you. She already knew these words too well, already knew they were insufficient. She would send them anyway.

gap_scenes.title: The First Cough
gap_scenes.text:
It began with a cough.

Isabelle was in her own apartment when she heard — a page had come with a message, and in the message was the information that the Archduke Charles Joseph had taken to his bed three days earlier with a fever, and that the fever was being attended to, and that there was no cause for alarm.

There was always cause for alarm when they said there was no cause for alarm.

She knew what smallpox did. She had grown up knowing it, had seen it in Italy, had heard the accounting of it from her father in the dry tone that people used when cataloguing losses that had already happened. She had been in Vienna long enough to see how much of this family's life was organized around grief and its anticipation.

She found Marie-Christine in the afternoon in the state drawing room, in conversation with Countess Vasquez, and she caught her eye and held it, and in the look that passed between them was the knowledge that they were both afraid of the same thing and could not say so in this room.

Later, alone for a few minutes in the corridor outside the gallery, Isabelle took Marie-Christine's hand without thinking about it — took it and held it, briefly, the pressure of palm against palm — and said nothing, and after a moment let go.

"I will tell you when I know more," Marie-Christine said quietly.

"I know you will," Isabelle said. "Go."

Marie-Christine went. Isabelle stood in the corridor and breathed slowly and wrote the first letter in her head before she had reached her own apartment.

gap_scenes.title: Night Watch
gap_scenes.text:
The palace had a different quality at two in the morning.

Isabelle had not been sleeping — had not been trying to sleep — and was sitting at her window wrapped in a shawl when she heard the soft footstep in the corridor that she recognized as belonging to Marie-Christine's particular way of moving at speed without appearing to hurry.

She went to her door.

Marie-Christine was still dressed, which meant she had not been to bed. Her face had the specific brightness of someone sustained by worry past all ordinary exhaustion, the eyes too alert, the color in her cheeks too high.

"He had a better night," she said, before Isabelle could speak. "The previous one was — it should have been worse than it was. But this one was better."

Isabelle stepped aside from the door. Marie-Christine came in and stood in the middle of the room and looked at the portraits on the wall with the unseeing gaze of someone whose mind is elsewhere. Isabelle brought two chairs close together near the window and sat down in one, and after a moment Marie-Christine sat down in the other.

They did not speak for a while. Outside, the city was dark and silent, and the sky had the particular thickness of a January night when snow might come.

"I'm making two portraits," Isabelle said finally. "Would you like one?"

Marie-Christine looked at her sideways. "Of whom?"

"You," Isabelle said. "From memory. I'll send you the better one when it's finished."

Marie-Christine put her face in her hands for a moment, not from grief but from something more complicated. Then she straightened and said: "Make it flattering."

"I can only make it true," Isabelle said, which was not quite an answer.

gap_scenes.title: After Charles
gap_scenes.text:
Archduke Charles Joseph died on January the eighteenth.

Isabelle had been in the room three corridors away when it happened, sitting with her hands folded in her lap and her face arranged into an expression that was supposed to convey composure, while internally she was conducting a conversation with God that was more in the nature of a negotiation. She had lost the negotiation.

The palace changed after. It changed in the way that palaces change after deaths — not dramatically, but in the molecular structure of it, the way people moved through rooms differently, spoke differently, assembled their faces differently. The Empress's grief was a fact of the building now, present in the walls.

Isabelle thought about death. She wrote to Marie-Christine about it — or tried to, writing several drafts and keeping none of them, because the thing she wanted to say was that death felt like a separation, and what she was most afraid of separating from was standing at the end of the corridor every morning looking at her over the heads of ladies-in-waiting.

She sent a note about an almanac instead. She sent it with a page who she knew was discreet.

The almanac was beautiful — she had annotated it with a private code she trusted Marie-Christine to read. Look for yourself in the print that represents marriage. I could not find you there. The absence in the picture felt like a kind of abandonment by the artist, and she wanted Marie-Christine to know that she had looked, specifically, with attention, and missed finding her.

The response came back within the hour. She read it standing in the corridor and did not wait to be somewhere private, which was unlike her, and also precisely appropriate.

gap_scenes.title: The Interval of Grief
gap_scenes.text:
There were three weeks in February when everything was gray.

Isabelle had learned that grief had textures, and the texture of the Habsburg court's grief was stone — slow, formal, expressed in black fabric and reduced ceremony and the particular silence of people who were accustomed to loss but not comfortable with it. The Empress wore her mourning as though it were armor. The Archduke Joseph moved through his days with the careful distance that had always been his register, now simply more pronounced.

Marie-Christine was different. She grieved actively, which surprised no one who knew her — she was not someone who performed emotion, but someone through whom it moved visibly, like weather through glass. Isabelle found her one afternoon sitting alone in the small salon off the gallery, not crying, simply sitting, with her hands in her lap and her eyes on the middle distance.

Isabelle sat down beside her without asking whether this was wanted.

After a while, Marie-Christine said: "Charles was the one I could talk to. Among the brothers."

"I know," Isabelle said. She didn't know, exactly, but she knew that it was true.

"I am tired of the ceremonies of grief," Marie-Christine said. "I want to be unhappy in an ordinary way, not in front of everyone."

Isabelle understood this profoundly. She had been unhappy in a very private way for weeks, not about Charles alone — she had barely known him — but about the proximity of death in general, and what it meant for the people she loved.

She reached out and took Marie-Christine's hand again. This time she held it longer, and Marie-Christine turned it palm-up and gripped hers in return.

gap_scenes.title: Your Hair, Her Health
gap_scenes.text:
The problem was not the hair, exactly.

Isabelle had arrived at Marie-Christine's apartment in great haste, because the morning had arranged itself into one of those brief intervals when the Empress was occupied and the ladies were scattered and there was, theoretically, twenty minutes of nothing. She had gone with no other intention than to be present, which was an intention that required no justification.

What she found was Marie-Christine at her dressing table, coughing.

It was not the first cough of the season — February was reliably unkind — but it was the cough that Isabelle had been hoping not to hear, the dry sustained kind that meant something had settled into the chest and intended to stay.

"You are not well," Isabelle said.

Marie-Christine waved a hand. "I am perfectly well."

"Your eyes are wrong."

"My eyes are always this color."

"The brightness is different. It's not good brightness."

Marie-Christine turned to look at her with the particular expression she reserved for being accurately diagnosed and refusing to enjoy it. Isabelle stood her ground.

"I came for twenty minutes," Isabelle said, "and now I am using them to be unhappy about your health instead of other things, which is very inconvenient."

"What other things?"

Isabelle did not answer this. She took the hairbrush from the dressing table and set it aside with the deliberateness of someone making a point, then sat on the edge of the bed and looked at her.

"Will you rest today?"

"Almost certainly not."

"I'll come back," Isabelle said, and meant everything by it.

gap_scenes.title: The Last Night of Carnival
gap_scenes.text:
The last day of Carnival was the last day before everything became serious.

Isabelle had always found this transition slightly absurd — that one could be, on Tuesday, a person in a mask attending a ball with an elaborately decorated agenda, and then, on Wednesday, someone undertaking forty days of reflection. But the absurdity was its own pleasure, the way that formal constraints made the space before them luminous.

She had spent part of the morning writing to Marie-Christine. She wrote standing up, with the desk too high, because she was almost ready to go out and was dressed and did not want to sit and crease anything. The message arrived at her hand before she'd finished composing it — Marie-Christine's handwriting, predictably, arriving at the exact moment of being thought about.

She read it. She wrote back. The exchange was the ordinary vocabulary of the everyday — where to meet, what hour, some information about the ball she would attend — and underneath it the other vocabulary, the one they used without using it, which was the vocabulary of being in the same city as each other.

That evening at the ball she moved through the rooms with Joseph's hand at the small of her back, and the music was very good, and she performed all the correct pleasures, and thought about Marie-Christine in the other wing of the palace, perhaps already at her evening prayers or perhaps reading, and felt the awareness of that location like a compass point.

She would tell her tomorrow about the lady she had seen — as beautiful as Venus, enormous and ridiculous — and make her laugh. The laughter would be real.

gap_scenes.title: Venus and the Jealous Divinity
gap_scenes.text:
She had told her about the lady at the ball and Marie-Christine had laughed exactly as expected, and the laughter had bent her forward over the table with her hand pressed to her mouth trying to contain it, and Isabelle had felt a pure and unreasonable pleasure that had nothing to do with the original story.

This was the difficulty.

The pleasure was not in the anecdote. The pleasure was always in the face receiving it.

They were sitting in Marie-Christine's apartment with the morning light coming in wrong through the curtains — too thin for February, too cold for brightness — and Isabelle had been there for an hour already, which was probably too long by any reasonable account of what she was supposed to be doing with a February morning. She did not particularly care.

Marie-Christine was talking about the opera. There was a question of whether to do something from it — one of the French pieces — and whether her voice was suited to the register, and Isabelle listened to the question and thought: your voice is suited to everything. This was not a helpful thought and she kept it to herself.

"It's a shame you don't sing French," Isabelle said instead. "There are operas that would suit you wonderfully."

Marie-Christine gave her a look. "You have never heard me sing."

"I have. Once, in the corridor, something you thought you were doing quietly."

The silence between this sentence and the next contained a great deal that neither of them named. Isabelle looked at the curtain. Marie-Christine looked at her hands.

"I adore you," Isabelle said, conversationally, as though it were a small thing.

"I know you do," Marie-Christine said, and neither of them looked away.

gap_scenes.title: The Morning Wait
gap_scenes.text:
She had been waiting for a quarter of an hour before she gave up and wrote a note instead.

The note was a very short note. It said: hello, adorable Sister, how are you? It said: I hope you slept well. It said: I cannot wait to hear from you. It did not say: I have been sitting here since I finished dressing, finding reasons not to leave for my own apartment, because the air in your corridor is preferable to the air anywhere else.

She folded the note. She thought about going down herself. She decided she would wait for permission, which was a convenient fiction she maintained in the intervals between being completely incapable of it.

The palace sounds moved through the walls in the particular rhythm of mid-morning: footsteps, voices at a distance, the creak of doors being opened and closed in some wing she couldn't see. The smell was cold stone and beeswax and, very faintly, the wood smoke from the fireplaces being tended in the staterooms.

She was in love with someone she could not be in love with in any acknowledged way, and the shape of this impossibility had become so familiar that she sometimes forgot to be troubled by it, and then remembered, and was briefly troubled, and then forgot again.

A page appeared at the end of the corridor and came toward her with a folded paper, which he offered.

She unfolded it before he had finished bowing. Marie-Christine's handwriting. Three words of greeting and then a question that invited her upstairs.

She gave the page a coin and went.

gap_scenes.title: The First Tears
gap_scenes.text:
She could not afterward reconstruct exactly what had caused it.

There had been an exchange — she and Marie-Christine, in the afternoon, in one of those conversations that began in one key and modulated without warning into another. They had been talking about something trivial. Then they had been talking about something else. Then something Marie-Christine had said — or hadn't said, or had said and immediately retreated from — had landed in Isabelle wrong, and she had felt the familiar pressure building behind her eyes that she ordinarily controlled with great efficiency.

She had not controlled it this time.

Marie-Christine had looked alarmed and then immediately guilty, which was not the intended effect. Isabelle had turned away toward the window and made herself breathe.

"I didn't mean —" Marie-Christine began.

"I know you didn't mean it," Isabelle said, which was not entirely true, and she heard the not-entirely-true quality in her own voice and tried to correct it. "It doesn't matter."

"It clearly does matter."

"You are making me sweat and cry which is too much," Isabelle said, and heard herself say it, and felt the absurdity of the sentence arrive a moment too late to prevent it, and then heard Marie-Christine make a sound that was half suppressed laugh and half genuine consternation.

"I'm sorry," Marie-Christine said.

"You're not," Isabelle said. "But you will be. I'm going to be very cruel to you for the rest of the afternoon."

"I believe you," Marie-Christine said, and moved closer, and Isabelle let her.

gap_scenes.title: Reconciliation in the Gallery
gap_scenes.text:
The gallery at Schönbrunn was too long for any ordinary conversation, which was precisely why they used it.

There was a protocol to these reconciliations. Isabelle had learned it over the winter: first the approach — measured, not quite indifferent — then the pause at some painting or object that required apparent consideration, then the conversation that began sideways and arrived, eventually, at the actual subject.

Today the subject was an argument that had been over for two days but not quite resolved, and they were both aware of it, and the awareness sat between them like a small fire that needed attending.

"Hello," Isabelle said. "Adorable Sister."

Marie-Christine glanced at her with an expression that contained amusement and also residual injury. "You've decided to be kind."

"I'm always kind. Except when I'm not, which is rare."

"That is entirely false."

"Almost entirely false," Isabelle conceded.

They walked together. The gallery was cold and long and full of gray March light that made everything look like a copy of itself. At the far end, one of the windows had a view of the formal gardens, brown still, waiting for spring.

"You make my head spin," Isabelle said eventually. "You make it spin continuously, which is exhausting, and I find I don't want to stop."

Marie-Christine was quiet for a step or two.

"That's almost an apology," she said.

"It's the best I can offer today," Isabelle said.

"Then I'll take it," Marie-Christine said, and the small fire went out, and the gallery felt warmer.

gap_scenes.title: The Sleepless Reading
gap_scenes.text:
At some point in the night she had finished the book.

Isabelle set it down on the covers and looked at the ceiling in the dark and thought about what she had just read. It was one of the reflective texts she had been studying — philosophy, loosely — and one passage in particular had lodged somewhere uncomfortable, a passage about the impossibility of knowing whether one's own feeling was true or merely constructed. She disagreed with it, and the disagreement had kept her awake, and now it was three in the morning and she was entirely alert.

She thought about sending it to Marie-Christine with a note. She thought about what the note would say.

The problem was that everything she wanted to say was contained inside the problem the text described. She felt things. Whether those feelings were what they seemed to be — whether the word she would use for them was accurate — this was the question, and it was a question she was not sure she needed philosophy to answer, because the answer was already there, had been there since October, and was not complicated.

She wrote a note and sealed it. The note said: I am in the worry that the reading I have done is causing me difficulty, and I cannot wait to see you and discuss it. She had not read quite that text, but the worry was real.

In the morning she would send it. Marie-Christine would understand which reading she meant and which she did not, because they had developed a vocabulary for this — a language made of references and half-allusions, the private syntax of two people who spoke to each other inside the official language of sisters-in-law.

She lay back and looked at the window and waited for dawn.

gap_scenes.title: Spring at Schönbrunn
gap_scenes.text:
April came to Schönbrunn slowly, with the reluctance of the north.

Isabelle had been in Vienna for six months now, and she understood the palace in a way she had not in October — understood its acoustics and its social weather, the way certain mornings predicted the shape of certain afternoons, the particular quality of light in each wing at different hours. She had also grown familiar with her own body in a new way: she was visibly pregnant now, which changed the texture of her days, the way people looked at her, the distances they kept.

Marie-Christine was not altered by it. This was one of the things Isabelle loved most.

Other people managed the pregnancy with a kind of careful reverence that Isabelle found exhausting — stepping back, adjusting their tone, treating her as though she had become both more important and more fragile simultaneously. Marie-Christine behaved as she always had: with directness, with humor, with the exacting attention of someone who was interested in the person and not the condition.

They walked in the garden on the afternoons when Isabelle felt well enough, which was most afternoons. The formal parterres of Schönbrunn were beginning to show their first color — tulips in the beds, the lime trees coming into their first pale green.

Marie-Christine walked beside her and talked about a book she had been reading, and a letter she had received, and something her mother had said, and Isabelle listened and felt the particular peace of being in the right place.

She was going to confession later. She would have to think carefully about what to say.

gap_scenes.title: Lisette and Linon
gap_scenes.text:
The game had started in a letter and continued in person, which was the best kind of game.

Isabelle had been calling herself Linon since June, which was the name of the young man in the comedy — the suitor, the lover, the one who was slightly absurd in his devotion. Marie-Christine was Lisette: the one who was adored. The roles were playful and also not playful, which was what made them work. Comedy was the only genre where you could say true things without being held responsible for them.

"Linon is in quite good condition this morning," Isabelle said, spreading her hands across the table, "and intends to offer you a gift."

Marie-Christine looked up from whatever she had been reading. "What kind of gift."

"A significant one. Not the sort Lisette could refuse without insulting Linon's feelings, which are very delicate."

"Linon's feelings are remarkably robust for something described as delicate."

"They are hidden behind a robust exterior, like certain buildings."

Marie-Christine lowered the paper and looked at her with the look that meant she was both refusing to laugh and definitely laughing. "What is the gift."

"Something in velvet," Isabelle said. "Don't ask me details. It's not ready yet. Let me do this."

She reached across the table and touched Marie-Christine's hand very briefly — the backs of her fingers against the back of Marie-Christine's, light as punctuation. Then she withdrew.

"We can see each other in half an hour," she said, standing. "In the meantime, I kiss you."

She left before the expression on Marie-Christine's face could become the specific kind that was hardest to walk away from.

gap_scenes.title: After the Quarrel
gap_scenes.text:
There were things that could be said in anger that could not afterward be unsaid.

Isabelle sat in her apartment for an hour after the fight — it had not been a fight, exactly, more a collapse of patience on both sides at once — and looked at the wall and reviewed what had been said, and found that some of it was unfair and some of it was accurate and some of it was simply the product of two people who had been too close together for too long in circumstances that did not allow for ordinary closeness.

The pregnancy made her sharp. She knew this and could not fully prevent it.

She had said things in the first movement — things she had recognized as wrong even as she was saying them — and Marie-Christine had looked at her with that expression that contained both injury and a refusal to be injured, which was somehow worse than simple hurt.

There was a page waiting outside the corridor. She sent him with nothing, which was also a message.

She thought about what she would write. How dare I appear before you after everything I am guilty of. She would say it plainly. She was good at plain speech when she decided to use it, and she had decided.

The summer afternoon outside was relentless: blue sky, green garden, the smell of cut grass coming through the window. Very unsuited to the interior weather.

She picked up her pen.

She wrote: I got angry. This is true. I am writing to ask you for justice, which is your friendship returned, which is all I want, which is what I have always wanted, which I should probably stop saying and simply demonstrate.

gap_scenes.title: The Tobacco Question
gap_scenes.text:
It had been Joseph who'd mentioned the tobacco, offhandedly, in a way that suggested he had not thought about whether to mention it, which meant he had thought about it carefully.

Isabelle had filed the information away and thought about it later. She did not especially want to know about Marie-Christine's habits through third parties. She would have preferred to discover them firsthand, which was the way she preferred to know everything about her.

The garden at Schönbrunn in summer was very large and very formal and very easy to get lost in if one wished to be lost. Isabelle had discovered several paths that led to small enclosed spaces planted with old roses, hot in the afternoon, where the wall blocked the sound of the palace.

She sat in one of these spaces now and turned her face up to the sun, which was a thing she was not supposed to do because of her complexion, and felt the heat press against her eyelids.

She thought about inconstancy. Whether she was inconstant was a genuine question — she changed her mind frequently about small things, preferences, opinions on literature. On the larger question she had not changed her mind since October, which was either constancy or stubbornness, and she was not certain of the distinction.

Marie-Christine was somewhere in the palace. They would see each other at the rosary. After the rosary, if the evening permitted, they might have a few minutes in the corridor.

Isabelle thought: a few minutes in the corridor is enough. She thought: it is not enough at all. These two thoughts were both true, which was the condition she seemed to live in permanently.

She went back inside to carry out whatever commissions she had been given.

gap_scenes.title: Zerbin Dreams of Laurette
gap_scenes.text:
In the mornings she often woke with the game still in her head — the roles, the names, the particular courtly register of the comedy that she and Marie-Christine had adopted as a second language for the things the first language couldn't hold.

Zerbin was the suitor in the piece they had been reading together and privately reassigning. He was devoted to the point of absurdity, which was both a joke and not a joke at all. Laurette received his devotion with the elegant slight cruelty of a woman who knew her own power, which was also both things at once.

Isabelle had woken this morning already writing the note in her head: I cannot help but ask how you slept. I cannot help but tell you that Zerbin dreams of his dear Laurette.

She was aware that this was not an especially dignified way to feel about one's sister-in-law. She had spent the first months in Vienna constructing arguments against the feeling, reviewing them, and discarding them as insufficient. The feeling did not require her approval to persist.

She wrote the note standing at her writing table, quickly, before the day organized itself into obligations. She folded it. She gave it to her most discreet maid.

She thought: there had been some fatigue yesterday. She thought: whatever happened that caused the fatigue, I am glad of it. She thought: this is probably the kind of thing that confessors want to hear about.

The maid returned with a note. Isabelle read it very fast and then again more slowly.

Laurette had slept well, the note said. Laurette was glad to hear from Zerbin. Laurette, in the margin, in smaller handwriting: I think of you too.

gap_scenes.title: The Tarantula
gap_scenes.text:
The restlessness had been there since morning.

Isabelle had tried to read and could not sit still. She had tried to draw and her hand moved wrong. She had walked to the end of her apartment and back several times, which was not enough room for the kind of walking that actually helped, and then had stood at the window looking out at the summer garden below, which was green and gold and entirely indifferent to her condition.

A tarantula bite, she had heard someone say once, produced exactly this: uncontrollable movement, the compulsion to dance, the inability to be still. She was not bitten by anything. She was simply insufficiently occupied and too aware of her own thoughts.

She had promised to leave for Holitsch at a certain time and was not going to be able to keep that promise. She needed to write and explain and also to ask whether the arrangement still held — the three-hour meeting, which was an unusual quantity of time for them to have together, and which she had been turning over in her mind for the past two days.

She sat down. She stood up.

Three hours was long enough to say things that required length. It was long enough to be in a room together without the conversation being conducted in code for the benefit of a third party. It was long enough to be ordinary — to simply be present, not in transit between two other things, not performing the intermediate space between obligation and obligation.

She sat down again and picked up her pen and wrote the note quickly: I will not have the grace to leave here as I promised. The tarantula bit me. Does the three-hour meeting still hold?

She sent it before she could revise it.

gap_scenes.title: The Garden at Dusk
gap_scenes.text:
She had not seen her all evening.

Isabelle had walked in the Schönbrunn garden in the early evening — the formal garden, then the path around the east end, then back along the parterre — and had not encountered Marie-Christine anywhere, which was not remarkable because the garden was large and the evening was warm and half the court was also somewhere in it. But she had looked.

Now she was back in her apartment, sitting at her writing table, and the garden outside was going dark in gradations of green and the swallows were making their last passes over the formal beds, and she was in a mood she could not entirely account for.

She opened the drawer and looked at her papers. She had been working on the second part of something — she was not certain what to call it, the piece she was writing, whether it was a theater piece or a meditation or simply a way of thinking on paper. It required a better mood than she presently had.

She thought: I would gladly trade this evening for a worse one somewhere better. She thought about the Waldenstein estates, which she had heard described, which sounded interminable. Even that seemed preferable to this particular shade of mood, which was the one caused by being in the same building as someone and not being near them.

She picked up her pen and wrote the opening of a note and then stopped, because what she wanted to write was: it was only not having seen you that made me feel this bad, and this was probably too much information for a note.

She folded it anyway and sent it, because too much information was still information.

gap_scenes.title: Separation
gap_scenes.text:
Marie-Christine had left for the country two days ago.

Isabelle was aware of this the way one is aware of a missing tooth — repeatedly, at intervals, each time with a small specific surprise at the absence.

The palace without her moved at a different speed. Isabelle attended the rosary, attended the Empress's morning reception, walked in the garden, sat for two hours with Madame d'Erdédy, who was pleasant and perceptive and not what she wanted. She ate meals at the correct tables and said the correct things and thought private thoughts behind a face she had trained to reveal nothing.

She had been working on the philosophical piece — the reflections, the thoughts about the situation of a young princess, about the court and the family and what one was supposed to feel and what one actually felt. She had written a section that she was almost pleased with and intended to share, but first she had shown it to the Empress by a chain of accidents too complicated to explain, and the Empress had not yet returned it.

This, too, felt like a small loss. Her own words, in transit, not quite belonging to her.

She wrote to Marie-Christine: the time seems very long to me, though it has not been long at all. I would like to be with you. She wrote about the heat she was not experiencing. She wrote about the Empress's response. She wrote: I started to speculate yesterday after reading your last note and wrote some thoughts that I intended to send you for fun.

The word fun was doing a great deal of work. She let it.

gap_scenes.title: The Reunion and the Rain
gap_scenes.text:
She had come back from the country with a complexion improved by outdoor air and an expression of someone who had been bored in extremely pleasant surroundings.

Isabelle had been watching from the window of the upper gallery when the carriage came through the gate, and had made herself wait a reasonable amount of time before going down, and then had gone down more quickly than reasonable.

In the first few minutes of reunion there was always the inventory — the involuntary assessment of whether the other person was still the same person, whether anything had changed in the interval. Marie-Christine passed this inspection easily. She was the same. The same quality of attention, the same quickness in the face, the same way of being in a room.

Then the weather had turned.

The late summer had gone gray and wet in a day, and the whole court had been driven indoors, where it conducted itself with the particular compressed energy of people deprived of their usual outlets. Isabelle found that music, which was ordinarily reliable, was not sufficient to improve her mood. She found that company helped only conditionally. She found that the only reliable remedy was the specific company she could not always arrange, and that arranging it was a logistics problem she spent a great deal of effort on.

"We will be together all day the day after tomorrow," Marie-Christine had said, "while the Empress is at Colloredo's."

Isabelle had received this information the way one receives a precise medical intervention — with relief, and with the secondary feeling that one should not have needed it quite so badly.

gap_scenes.title: The Rosary and the Chest
gap_scenes.text:
She had talked about Marie-Christine for too long.

This was the problem with love, she had begun to understand: it produced speech. Not useful speech, not the speech of information or negotiation, but the exhausting, circular speech of someone who was working something out by sound and needed an audience. The audience in this case had been kind enough, one of her ladies, and Isabelle had talked for perhaps twenty minutes and then noticed the polite attentiveness of someone who was performing interest, and had stopped.

But by then the damage was done. Her chest was dried out from talking, a specific physical exhaustion that required barley water and rest.

She had attended the rosary afterward anyway, because the rosary was required, and had stood in the correct position and said the correct words and had, in the privacy of the prayers, conducted a parallel and rather different conversation with God.

The conversation with God was about the nature of virtue and the question of whether she was practicing it. She was twenty years old now. She was a wife and was beginning to be a mother. She was in love with her husband's sister in a way that she recognized as requiring either renaming or accepting, and she was not prepared to do either with any conviction.

She had resolved, coming back from the rosary, to be more measured. To be sensible. To be twenty, as the age required.

She was going to write Marie-Christine a very contained and reasonable note, she decided.

She was not sure this would work, but she was going to try it, because the barley water had helped and her chest was feeling better and she was feeling very nearly wise.

gap_scenes.title: The New Year at Twenty
gap_scenes.text:
The year turned and Isabelle was twenty years old.

This was not in itself remarkable. Many people turned twenty. The remarkable part was that she had expected it to feel different — to feel like the acquisition of some additional gravity, some wisdom she had been promised would arrive with the decade's turn — and instead she felt exactly the same, which was both a relief and a minor disappointment.

The winter had settled over Schönbrunn with its usual indifference. She had attended the New Year's ceremonies with the composed seriousness that was her public face, and afterward had gone to her apartment and sat at the window and thought about the previous New Year, which had been her nineteenth birthday, which had been the first New Year in Vienna, which had been the year everything had started.

Marie-Christine had been at the ceremony but they had not had a chance to speak. They exchanged looks across the room, which was the ordinary ration.

She thought about what she had written the previous January: that she thought about death, and that the thought of it was a separation, and that there was one separation she could not face. The thought was still true. She was not sure what to do with thoughts that stayed true.

The Empress was unwell — a headache, nothing serious, already improving by the time the evening dispatches came. Isabelle had been watching her closely. The Empress was the architecture of this whole life, the foundation under every arrangement, and foundations should not crack.

She went to check on Marie-Christine, because this was what she did, because it was December and the year was ending and some habits had become structural.

gap_scenes.title: Ferdinand's Fever
gap_scenes.text:
It came in January, which was the month that had already taken too much.

Isabelle heard about the Archduke Ferdinand's illness through the ordinary channels — a message, a medical attendant speaking to the Empress's household — and felt the familiar cold recognition settle in her chest. She had been here before. She knew what this looked like from the outside: the careful bulletins, the optimistic language that was itself a kind of warning, the way the palace reorganized itself around a single sick room.

She went to find Marie-Christine.

She found her in the corridor outside the family apartments, already in motion, already managing the information and the household responses with the focused calm that Isabelle had come to recognize as her mode under pressure. Marie-Christine was efficient in crises the way she was warm in ordinary time — fully, without reservation.

"Tell me what you know," Isabelle said.

Marie-Christine told her. The evacuation, the stomach tension, the first night's sleep. They walked while she spoke, turning the information into action by virtue of moving.

"I cannot say anything until morning," Marie-Christine said.

"Then I'll wait for morning," Isabelle said.

They stood for a moment at the junction of two corridors, in the particular cold that lived in the old parts of the palace in January. Isabelle thought about the previous January. She thought: we have survived this before. She did not say it, because it was not yet true.

"Go," Isabelle said. "I'll write to you tonight."

"You don't have to."

"I want to," Isabelle said. "Farewell."

gap_scenes.title: What Writing Cannot Say
gap_scenes.text:
Ferdinand had improved, and then improved further, and by the second week of February was well enough for the household to exhale.

Isabelle had written three letters during the crisis: one practical, one affectionate, one that she had not sent and had burned instead, because it said too much. The letters she had sent were the correct kind — attentive, tender, restrained. The letter she had burned was something else.

Now it was February, and the crisis had passed, and she was writing again in the ordinary mode, which was the mode she preferred because it had more room in it.

Her chest was still exhausted from the previous weeks — the talking, the vigilance, the particular physical cost of sustained anxiety. She had decided to write what she could not say aloud, which was a reversal of her usual method. Usually the letters were the restrained version. Today they were the only version she could manage.

She wrote: until I can have the pleasure of going to your house, I cannot help writing to you. I believe it is easier to talk to you in writing about certain things. When we see each other, all the most beautiful ideas give way to the desire to simply be present.

She read this back. It was not quite accurate — the desire to be present was itself one of the most beautiful ideas. But she let it stand because it was moving in the right direction.

She sealed the letter and sent it and went to get dressed to go upstairs, because writing was only the preparation, and the preparation was not the thing itself.

gap_scenes.title: This Morning, This Once
gap_scenes.text:
She had come in the morning, which was the best time — before the day's obligations had fully materialized, when the palace had the particular quiet of an engine not yet running.

Marie-Christine had been at her writing table, not yet dressed, which was an intimacy that Isabelle had grown accustomed to without growing less aware of it. The informality of a person before they had assembled their public face. She valued this access more than she ever said.

They had talked for an hour. Not about anything important — or rather, about things that were important in a quiet way, the private architecture of their shared daily life. About Marie-Anne, and certain precautions Isabelle thought wise. About the court's weather, who was reliable, who was not. About a letter from the country that had contained some news.

She had kissed Marie-Christine at some point — on the cheek, a greeting, an ordinary thing, unremarkable except in the particular way that it was never entirely unremarkable, which was a distinction she kept to herself.

By late morning she had her own matters to attend to. She sent a short note as she left — having had you this morning, I will not call you again, there is work — but left the door open on an if: unless there is a reason. Unless you want me. Unless the afternoon permits.

She went to her apartment and picked up where she had left off with whatever needed doing, and thought: that was a good morning. She thought this as a straightforward evaluation of evidence, without qualification.

A good morning. She would have another one, if the afternoon permitted.

gap_scenes.title: The Dancing Child
gap_scenes.text:
Something moved against her ribs at evening prayer.

Isabelle had been kneeling in the correct position, hands folded, mouth producing the correct responses, when the baby kicked — a real kick, sudden and definite — and she had felt it travel through her whole body like a small percussion, and had gripped the pew with both hands and breathed.

She was five months or thereabouts. The doctors gave different estimates. What she knew was that it was present, increasingly, with an agenda of its own.

She told Marie-Christine afterward, in the corridor, in three sentences. Marie-Christine had put her hand on Isabelle's arm and said "show me" and Isabelle had guided her hand to the right place, and then the baby had done absolutely nothing at all for a full minute, as though performing its refusal to perform, and then had moved again, and Marie-Christine had looked up with an expression of pure surprise that Isabelle found herself wanting to preserve somehow.

Later, in her apartment, she wrote about it — not to Marie-Christine directly, because she had already seen her, but in the notes she kept for herself, the record she was building of what it felt like to be in this body in this time.

"My youngster danced against my stomach," she wrote. "It was almost too much."

She thought about the word almost. She left it.

That evening, at the Empress's sofa, she had lain down for a few minutes — the nausea had come back briefly — and thought about what it meant to be building two things simultaneously: a child and a love. She was not sure they were separate projects.

gap_scenes.title: The Stubborn Note
gap_scenes.text:
There are days when a small obstinacy is the only freedom available.

Isabelle had been told something — kindly, by someone meaning well — that she considered incorrect, and she had said as much, and the conversation had ended in the particular way that conversations end when one party simply declines to concede regardless of the argument's quality.

She had been in this mood all afternoon.

She wrote a note to Marie-Christine that was almost nothing: three sentences on a quarter-sheet of paper, delivered by the page who waited in the antechamber. The note said approximately: with donkeys — and she meant herself here, and also perhaps Marie-Christine, because the category was large — one must use a certain patience. She was not feeling patient. She was feeling extremely stubborn and somewhat entertained by her own stubbornness, which was better than the alternative.

The note was a declaration of intent more than a communication. It said: I am in a mood and I am going to be in it and I will repay whatever slight has occasioned the mood when the opportunity presents itself.

Marie-Christine would understand. She always understood the notes that seemed to not quite mean anything, because they had been communicating in this register for over a year now, and the register had its own grammar.

She sent it and felt better. The mood did not lift exactly but it reorganized itself into something more bearable — the particular comfort of being known well enough that even a letter about nothing is still a letter to someone who will read it correctly.

gap_scenes.title: Baadwaschl
gap_scenes.text:
She had learned the word two days ago.

One of the younger ladies had used it — a Viennese term, slang, meaning something like washcloth, or alternatively a kind of wet, limp uselessness — and Isabelle had written it down phonetically and then deployed it in the wrong context and been corrected and then deployed it correctly in a note to Marie-Christine, who had laughed in person when she saw it, which was the best outcome.

Marie-Christine had taken to the idea enthusiastically, which was characteristic: she engaged with language the way she engaged with music, quickly and with a particular proprietary delight.

"Write it to me," she had said. "In the letter. I want to see it."

Isabelle thought: I am going to write you a very short letter in which I call you a Viennese slang word for a washcloth and this will apparently give you great joy, and I will do this because giving you great joy is a goal I pursue with considerably more dedication than most of my other goals.

She picked up her pen. She thought about the most beautiful things she had to say, which were numerous and which required precisely the opposite of brevity. She would not write those things. She would write the short letter with the absurd word and the joy it produced would be real, which was the thing that mattered.

Oh my Gne, she wrote — their shared nonsense-word, their private nothing-word — because I am also a donkey.

She wrote the word. She wrote: I am completely obedient to you and will call you this from now on, because it gives you such joy.

And this too — the obedience, the calling, the joy — was the truest thing she had written all week.

gap_scenes.title: Two Languages for One Thing
gap_scenes.text:
She had been ill for four days.

Nothing dramatic — a cold that had settled into the chest, a quality of general diminishment that the body produces when it has been asked to do too much in too cold a month. She had stayed in her apartment for two days, which was the concession, and then had resumed most of her ordinary life, which was perhaps too fast.

The notes from Marie-Christine during this interval had been more frequent than usual. Isabelle had read them in bed, sitting up against her pillows, and had written back when she was well enough to hold a pen without her handwriting looking like a different person's.

Marie-Christine had been worried. Isabelle knew this not from anything explicit but from the particular quality of the notes — the frequency, the slight formal excess that appeared when Marie-Christine was trying not to show concern and showing it anyway.

The note that arrived on the fourth day had a postscript in three languages: Italian, then German, then Spanish. Isabelle read it twice and understood that what was being said in three languages was the same thing said three ways, with the redundancy being the message: I rejoice. I want to tell you again that I love you. I desire that this continues always.

She held the paper against her chest for a moment — the paper and its three languages and what they amounted to — and then set it carefully in the box where she kept the letters she was not going to burn.

She wrote back: hello, my favorite. I am doing well. Better than well. The Khevenhüller has brought you good luck, and I hope it continues, and here are two languages that could confuse anyone, so I will say simply: I am dying of love for you.

gap_scenes.title: The Furniture Left Behind
gap_scenes.text:
The note had been brief — barely a dozen lines — and Isabelle read it twice before setting it on the table beside her untouched cup of chocolate. Outside, the Vienna afternoon was the colour of pewter, and a thin rain tapped at the glass as though asking to be admitted.

She had accused her of forgetting. That was the word that stung: forgetting. As if anything to do with Marie-Christine could be forgotten, as if it were possible to misplace the fact of her, the weight of her presence in a room, the particular quality of silence that followed when she left it.

Isabelle crossed to the window. Below, a footman hurried across the courtyard with his hat pressed to his head, and she watched him disappear under an arch. The furniture in question — a small writing table, a chair with a cushion of green silk — remained where she had left them, and they remained there deliberately. It was the only piece of a conversation she could carry with her from one apartment to another without anyone knowing it for what it was.

She wrote back immediately, defending herself in that quick tumbling way she had, half laughing, half indignant. You would be right on Saturday but today you are wrong. She said the words aloud to herself as she wrote them, and something loosened in her chest.

She was always wrong to love so indiscreetly. And she was always wrong to stop.

gap_scenes.title: The Morning of March Twentieth
gap_scenes.text:
She had not expected joy to feel so much like exhaustion. The hours before dawn had been long and painful, and she had gripped the bedpost and thought of nothing at all, which was the only thing one could do. Afterwards she lay still for a very long time, listening to the fire breathe in the grate.

The chamberwomen moved around her quietly, and she let them. She was thinking about Marie-Christine, who was somewhere in the palace at this moment, perhaps awake, perhaps not yet knowing.

Isabelle composed the letter in her head before she was well enough to sit up and write it. She wanted to describe the feeling — this extraordinary ordinary triumph of simply continuing to exist, of having passed through the worst of it and come out on the other side into a pale morning that contained, improbably, herself in it still. The body's comedy. The body's relentless forward motion.

When she finally took the pen in her hand, the words arrived quickly, giddy with relief. She was at the height of joy. She wanted Marie-Christine to judge her contentment, to feel what she felt, to share this obscure domestic victory over fear.

She sealed the letter and sent it before she had finished her broth. To wait would have seemed impossible. Every hour Marie-Christine did not know was an hour wasted.

gap_scenes.title: The Night Between
gap_scenes.text:
She slept for most of the rest of the twentieth, deeply and without dreams, which was itself a kind of grace. When she woke the candles had burned low and someone had placed a fresh blanket over her and left a small lamp burning on the chest near the door.

For a moment she did not know where she was — or rather, she knew it perfectly well, but for an instant she was suspended between sleep and waking in a condition that felt like the absence of all trouble. The room smelled of beeswax and something faintly bitter from the medicine on the nightstand.

Then it all came back, softly, without alarm. She was well. She had written to Marie-Christine. There would be an answer, perhaps tomorrow, perhaps a note slipped under the door before morning.

She thought of what it would feel like to be fat again, as she had written — the word making her smile even now. Fat and visible and present, not just this diminished, aching thing pressed under blankets. She thought of going down to dinner, of sitting in the ordinary lamplight of the evening, of the pleasure of being looked at by someone who looked at her as though she were the whole room.

She would be as much in evidence as possible tomorrow. She was already composing what she would say.

gap_scenes.title: Confinement
gap_scenes.text:
By the following afternoon Isabelle had decided that recovery was, in many respects, more tedious than illness itself. At least illness made demands of you. Recovery simply required you to sit still and wait for time to pass, which was the one thing she had never been able to do well.

Gautier had been in to attend to the housekeeping of her body, which Isabelle submitted to with the impatient stoicism of someone who has learned that the body does not negotiate. Then she had sat by the window in a dressing gown and watched the courtyard and written half a letter and abandoned it and begun another.

She could hear voices somewhere in the corridor — the characteristic sound of the palace going about its business without her, which it did with perfect indifference. She was not yet well enough to leave her apartment, and this fact imposed a particular kind of solitude that she found, depending on the hour, either peaceful or maddening.

What she wanted, plainly and with a force that embarrassed her slightly to acknowledge, was company. One person's company. But there were rules about visiting chambers in the aftermath of confinement, rules designed by people who had clearly never experienced the specific desolation of being left alone with nothing but their own thoughts and the sound of rain on the palace roof.

She picked up the pen again and resumed the letter.

gap_scenes.title: Word from the Opera
gap_scenes.text:
Someone had mentioned in passing that a certain singer would perform that week — she could not recall the name now, only the way it had been said, with a particular brightness that suggested the news was considered an event.

Isabelle turned the information over in her mind all evening. She would perhaps be well enough to attend, or perhaps not. The physician would have opinions, which she would consider seriously and then largely disregard, because she had found that her own assessment of her condition tended to be more accurate than theirs when the condition in question was boredom.

Spring was beginning to be felt in the city, in the particular quality of light in the late afternoon and the slight loosening of the air that came with it. She had been inside too long. Her body registered this as a kind of low continuous complaint, a restlessness that had nowhere to go.

She thought about the prospect of sitting in a box at the opera with Marie-Christine close enough to touch. The music would be something Italian, something ornate and sorrowful and completely unsuited to its surroundings. She would pretend to follow the libretto and instead watch the light on Marie-Christine's face when the soprano held a phrase too long.

The thought was almost enough. She sent a note asking whether they might go together. She signed it simply with an I and waited for the answer with more composure than she actually felt.

gap_scenes.title: Eckartsau, the Night Before
gap_scenes.text:
The imperial hunting lodge at Eckartsau sat at the edge of the Marchfeld where the Danube bent east, and in early summer it smelled of pine resin and river water and the particular mineral coldness of the marshes at dusk.

Isabelle had arrived with the party in the late afternoon, and now she stood at the window of the room they had given her and watched the light drain out of the sky over the floodplains. The horses were still being stabled below; she could hear their voices, that distinctive low conversation between men and animals that the darkness brought out.

Tomorrow there would be hunting, and mass before hunting, and then the long return journey. The Painter — Liotard, she thought, that Swiss oddity with his extraordinary eyes — had been at supper and talked the whole time in that rapid pleasant way that filled every silence and asked nothing of you in return. She had been grateful. She had needed not to be the most talkative person in the room for once.

But the reason she was standing at this window at this hour, not sleeping, was simpler than all of that. She had left Vienna this morning, and the leaving had undone her more than she had expected. Not the leaving itself — she had managed that with adequate dignity — but the moment just before, when she had turned at the door and Marie-Christine had been watching her from across the room, and had not said anything, and neither had she.

She pressed her forehead against the cool glass. Somewhere in the wetlands a bird called once and was silent.

gap_scenes.title: Autumn at the Margins of the Hunt
gap_scenes.text:
The boar hunt was the court's annual ritual of controlled violence, and Isabelle had learned in three years of attending it that her role was primarily to be present and not to ask awkward questions about the animals. She sat in a wooden blind at the forest's edge with two other ladies and watched the men move through the trees like figures in a tapestry — purposeful, decorated, absorbed in their purpose.

She was thinking about Marie-Christine, who was somewhere back at the lodge, which was infuriating. The whole pleasure of these excursions — the only pleasure, she amended honestly — was the stolen proximity they offered, the legitimacy of sitting close in a carriage, the shared vocabulary of complaint about the cold.

The great boar was brought down with a shot that startled the birds out of the canopy for a long moment. The men called to each other. Someone blew a horn. The ritual required enthusiasm, and she produced it, and it was received as genuine because she produced it well.

But in her hut that evening, eating cold meat and listening to the wind in the pines, she composed in her head the letter she would send in the morning. I sigh in my hut after the happiness of seeing you again. She would write that, she decided. It was true, and the truth of it made her feel both better and worse, in the way that accurate language often did.

gap_scenes.title: Orpheus and Eurydice
gap_scenes.text:
The opera was Gluck's, new and strange, and the Burgtheater held it at a temperature that made the candle smoke rise without dissipating, so that by the second act the air above the audience was gauzy and warm.

Isabelle sat between the Archduke and her brother Leopold, which was precisely what she had arranged, and was precisely as unsatisfying as she had known it would be. Across the house she was aware of Marie-Christine without looking at her — aware in the way one is aware of a fire in a room even with one's back to it.

Orpheus was descending for the second time into the underworld, and the music was doing something to the theatre that theatre did not often manage — opening it up from the inside, creating in the gilded room a sudden improbable sincerity. Isabelle found that her throat had tightened.

What has become of my dear Eurydice? She did not say the words aloud but she thought them, and they arrived already weighted with something that had nothing to do with Greek mythology. The idea that Marie-Christine was mortal — that she would die someday, as everyone would, as Archduchess Jeanne might yet, as Isabelle herself sometimes felt she would — was not a new thought, but the music made it vivid and close.

She did not cry. She was between the Archduke and her brother, and one did not cry in the theatre. But she sat very still for a long time, and the music went on without asking her permission.

gap_scenes.title: The Empress's Composure
gap_scenes.text:
It was her sister Marie-Anne who said, the following morning, that the Empress had not cried once at the previous evening's entertainment, which she offered as evidence of her mother's remarkable self-mastery.

Isabelle listened to this with her cup halfway to her lips. She had her own theory about the Empress's self-mastery, which was that it was less composure than determination, less peace than the permanent condition of a woman who had held an empire together with her own two hands while bearing sixteen children and had concluded somewhere along the way that she could not afford the luxury of private feeling.

But this was not a theory she expressed aloud, because it would have been imprudent and also because she was uncertain she believed it entirely. The Empress might simply have found Gluck unpersuasive.

The late October light came through the high windows of the breakfast room at an angle that flattened everything, made the faces around the table look like a painting of themselves. Isabelle thought about Marie-Christine's face at the opera — she had looked once, deliberately and briefly, in the second act — and the particular quality of attention Marie-Christine gave to music, as though she were in conversation with it.

She thought about crying in theatres and about the people worth crying for and about the specific mercy of being able to write instead of having to speak. She reached for the bread.

gap_scenes.title: The Portrait in Words
gap_scenes.text:
She had been trying for weeks to describe her — not in letters, where the code of tenderness already had its established register, but in something more systematic. A portrait in language, she thought, as Liotard made portraits in pastel: accurate, flattering, honest in a way that flattery sometimes accidentally was.

She sat at her writing table with the papers from her chaotic drawer fanned around her — the political writing she did not remember writing, the comic opera in three scenes, the moral reflections, the harpsichord exercises. All the evidence of a mind that moved too quickly and in too many directions at once.

Beautiful eyes. That was where she started, because it was where one always started with Marie-Christine, the eyes being the first thing one encountered and the last thing one forgot.
