Hair of the same colour. A pretty mouth. A beautiful throat. She wrote these things with the care of someone handling something that might break if set down too quickly.

Then the more difficult observations. She liked to torment, and was sorry the moment she succeeded. She formed opinions of people too quickly and held them too long. She spoke of her own death too readily, which upset those who loved her and deserved better than to be frightened on a Tuesday afternoon.

Isabelle paused over this last one. Then she left it in. It was the most sincere sentence in the whole portrait, and the most obviously written by someone who had stood at the edge of that particular conversation and felt the ground shift beneath her feet.

gap_scenes.title: Vigil
gap_scenes.text:
Archduchess Jeanne was seventeen years old and had been beautiful in the way that the very young sometimes were, all freshness and unearned confidence, before they have been taught to moderate themselves. Now she lay in her bed with a fever that had been climbing since the second week of November, and the physicians came and went with their grave faces and their cautious language, and the family waited.

Isabelle had been waiting in the particular way she waited for things she could not control, which was to say she kept writing. Notes at odd hours, scraps of thought sent across the palace by whichever servant could be pressed into service. She monitored the fever's progress the way she would have monitored weather approaching from the west — with attention, with knowledge that nothing she did would alter its course, with the specific helplessness of the intelligent before the indifferent.

At night she could not sleep. This was not the ordinary insomnia of an anxious mind but something more physical, a wakefulness imposed from outside, as though the palace itself were sitting up.

Marie-Christine was her closest correspondent in all of this — the one she told everything, the one whose news she demanded every morning before she had properly risen. The illness moving through the apartments of the Hofburg had a particular intimacy, a closeness that frightened her, and the letters were the only place she could say so clearly.

She lay in the dark and counted the hours and waited for morning.

gap_scenes.title: The Feast of Saint Immaculata
gap_scenes.text:
December the eighth was Marie-Christine's name day, and also the Feast of the Immaculate Conception, and also — Isabelle had checked — the eleventh day of Jeanne's illness, and the physicians had said that the fourteenth day would be decisive.

She had calculated this against the calendar several times, as though repetition might change the arithmetic. It did not.

The corridor outside her apartment was cold in the particular way December corridors in the Hofburg were cold: a dampness that lived in the walls and could not be entirely defeated by any number of fires. She had put on two shawls over her dressing gown and still felt it.

She was writing Marie-Christine's name-day letter, which required a balance she was still attempting to achieve between celebration and anxiety. She loved Marie-Christine beyond her capacity to express it, which was saying something since her capacity to express things was considerable. She also needed to tell her about Jeanne, who had slept badly the night before, whose fever had not broken.

But the day was Marie-Christine's day. Vasquez would be wishing her well, and Isabelle wished it too, sincerely and with an urgency that had nothing to do with ceremony — wished her well in the largest possible sense of the word, wished her years and ease and the kind of happiness that doesn't require an occasion to be observed.

She wrote: I love you beyond everything I can say.

gap_scenes.title: The Consultation
gap_scenes.text:
Van Swieten arrived at two o'clock in the afternoon with the expression he wore when he had information he did not wish to give, which was an expression that could be mistaken for ordinary sternness unless you had seen it before.

Isabelle had seen it before. She watched from the doorway of the anteroom as he spoke to the Empress in the low precise way that physicians used to deliver news without technically saying anything definitive. The Empress stood very straight, which meant she was frightened.

Jeanne had spoken all night in languages that were not French and sometimes were not any language at all. She was terribly hot. There had been no sweat, which was the thing that mattered and which everyone was too careful to say directly.

Isabelle withdrew to her own apartment and sat at her table and wrote to Marie-Christine. She wrote quickly, as she always did when the thing she was writing was serious — not because haste made the words better but because haste prevented her from stopping to consider whether she should write them at all.

She wrote: watch out for a scene like two years ago. The allusion was to the Archduke Charles, who had died of smallpox when Isabelle had only just arrived in Vienna, who had been gone before she could quite grasp what a family it was she had married into. The empire that swallowed its children and kept moving forward.

She wrote: I cannot say anything. Farewell. She meant it both ways.

gap_scenes.title: The Night of the Third Week
gap_scenes.text:
Jeanne had slept. Not peacefully — even in sleep she moved and murmured, her hands working at the coverlet — but she had slept, which was more than the night before.

Isabelle had been to see her, briefly and at a careful distance, and had stood in the doorway looking at this girl who was seventeen and had been lovely and was now diminished to something urgent and fragile and entirely herself in the way that illness stripped everything extraneous from a person. She felt a tenderness for her that she had not known was there.

She went back to her own rooms and found that her joints ached, a new and slightly alarming development she would mention to no one. The cold in the apartments and the disrupted sleep and the long days of waiting had accumulated in her body as stiffness, as a deep fatigue that sleep did not entirely relieve.

But Jeanne was sleeping longer, the intervals between waking growing. The fever had not left but had steadied. Van Swieten drew conclusions he refused to share outright, which Isabelle took to mean that the conclusions were not entirely negative.

She went to her writing table. She wrote to Marie-Christine that she was starting to hope. She wrote that she was embracing her with all her heart, because with all her strength would not be saying much — which was true. She wrote that she adored her to a point she could not express and which made her tremble for her life at the slightest inconvenience.

All of this was true. All of it together in one letter seemed almost too much. She sent it anyway.

gap_scenes.title: The Twenty-Third of December
gap_scenes.text:
Archduchess Jeanne died on the twenty-third of December, 1762. She was seventeen years old. She had been ill for thirty-two days.

Isabelle sat in her apartment for a long time after they told her, not moving, with her hands in her lap in the attitude of a person who is waiting for something to happen that has already happened. Outside, the courtyard was quiet in the particular way that courts went quiet when the news had not yet spread to the outermost rooms and the carriages and the kitchens.

She thought about her sister-in-law Marie-Christine, who was somewhere in these same corridors, who had lost a sister. She thought about what it would mean to lose a sister and understood it only partly, because her own sisters were elsewhere, in Parma, in a different life. But she had Marie-Christine, and the thought of losing Marie-Christine was so immediate and so vast that she could not hold it.

Christmas Eve was tomorrow. Easter would be April the third. These were the fixed points of the calendar, indifferent and enduring.

She did not write that evening. There was nothing to say that was adequate, and she had always preferred silence to inadequacy. But she sent someone to ask how Marie-Christine was, and she lay awake listening to the palace settle and reform around this new absence in it, this new cold room at the center of the family.

In the morning she would write. She always wrote in the morning.

gap_scenes.title: The Year Turning
gap_scenes.text:
The new year arrived without ceremony, which suited Isabelle well enough. She had attended mass and had not enjoyed it, which was a pattern she had come to accept about her religious feeling: it required solitude and silence and the absence of anyone she was supposed to impress.

Jeanne's rooms were being cleared. This was the way of courts: grief had its ceremonial expression and then the apartments were needed for something else, and practicality reasserted itself over sentiment with its usual gentle brutality. Isabelle watched the servants carry things out and thought about time and how it moved.

She had been to the opera — she could not now have said which one — and had found herself sitting in the dim warmth of the box in a state that was not quite grief and not quite peace but something that moved between them. The music had been very beautiful. She had been better during it than after.

The wildest thoughts, she wrote in her letter to Marie-Christine. She had not yet sent it. She had written it and then folded it and then unfolded it and looked at the line again. The wildest thoughts have not yet dissipated. It was true. It would have been truer to say that grief and desire and the January cold and the persistent ache in her joints had combined into something she did not have a precise name for, something that made the ordinary world feel both very close and very far.

I will come to see you. She added that at the end and sealed it quickly before she could revise it.

gap_scenes.title: After the Miscarriage
gap_scenes.text:
The thing she had hoped for had not been allowed to continue. This was how she thought of it, in the days after: not as a loss but as a permission withdrawn, as though whatever determined these things had reconsidered and taken it back. The language of denial rather than grief. It was easier, just barely.

Van Swieten had come, and afterwards she had slept a great deal, and in her sleep she had dreamed with an insistence and vividness that exhausted her further, dreams in which she was looking for things she could not name in rooms she did not recognize.

Marie-Christine sent notes. This was the kindness she was best at, the persistent evidence of attention, the refusal to leave a silence unfilled for too long. Isabelle received each one with a feeling she could not properly articulate, which was part gratitude and part the particular ache of being cared for by someone you loved more than they knew.

She was not well. Her chest was tired, her joints ached, she woke in the night coughing. The winter had settled into her body as though it intended to stay. But she was awake, and she was writing, and somewhere in the palace Marie-Christine was awake too, and that had always been, and remained, the essential fact.

She wrote a long letter that covered everything and nothing in the way her letters often did, spiraling around the center of things without quite landing on them. Then she sent it and went to the window and looked out at the January courtyard and breathed.

gap_scenes.title: February's Long Middle
gap_scenes.text:
February in Vienna was not a month that invited much beyond endurance. The light came late and left early and in between offered very little by way of compensation. The gardens at Schönbrunn were bare and formal, their geometry stripped to its most rigorous argument.

Isabelle walked when she was able and lay down when she was not, and in between wrote letters to Marie-Christine that were the most honest account of her interior life available to her. She told her about the dreams, the coughing, the nights she slept in fits and woke to the sound of her own breathing. She did not tell her how frightened she sometimes was at the frequency of all of this, because to say so would have been to frighten Marie-Christine, and the protection of that particular peace in her — even the peace of ordinary worry rather than serious alarm — felt like a task Isabelle had assigned herself without quite deciding to.

On a February afternoon she looked at herself in the glass for a long time and thought: you look like someone who has been ill. She had never cared very much about what she looked like, but she cared about what she conveyed, and what she conveyed at present was a fragility she resented.

She went back to her writing table. She had a letter half-composed, something cheerful and slightly exasperated, the tone she deployed when things were difficult and she did not want anyone to know. She finished it and sealed it. Tomorrow she would perhaps be able to go to Marie-Christine's rooms.

Perhaps tomorrow.

gap_scenes.title: The Marshmallow Paste
gap_scenes.text:
She had eaten the marshmallow paste at two in the morning, in the dark, sitting upright in bed with her nightgown twisted around her and the cough finally giving way after what felt like long enough to cross a small country.

And then silence, and the particular surprised quality of a body that has been fighting something and has suddenly won, and then sleep, deep and dreamless, until seven.

She woke feeling almost human. This was a condition that came and went now with a frequency that should perhaps have alarmed her more than it did, but she had found that she adapted quickly to impermanence, that she had become good at locating happiness in whatever intervals it occupied.

She dressed quickly and wrote to Marie-Christine before breakfast. The tone of the letter was one she had perfected over two and a half years of correspondence: lightly comic, affectionate, scattering observations in every direction like a woman shaking out a tablecloth. The substance of it was: I am here. I slept. I think of you.

The reply would come before noon if the morning went well. It usually did. There was a rhythm to their correspondence that had become as structural as architecture, as reliable as walls.

She ate breakfast and listened to the sounds of the palace waking around her and felt, with an intensity that sometimes still surprised her, how much of her happiness lived outside her own body, in another room, in another person's continued existence.

gap_scenes.title: Dinner at Her Place
gap_scenes.text:
The Archduke had gone for his ride, which meant the afternoon had a particular quality of spaciousness that Isabelle associated with freedom, though she would not have used that word aloud.

She had sent the note — come to dinner, invite my sister Marie-Anne — and then immediately began wishing she had not invited Marie-Anne, who had excellent qualities but was not the company she wanted at this particular table on this particular day. She wanted Marie-Christine across from her, only Marie-Christine, with the afternoon light on the tablecloth and the ordinary sounds of the palace going about its business beyond the door.

But one did not say that. One said: dinner at my place, invite the others, because the others made it a normal occasion and a normal occasion did not require explanation.

She set the table herself, or supervised its setting with more attention than the task strictly required, adjusting the position of a candlestick twice. She had been coughing again, a dry ineffectual cough that did nothing for her and bothered everyone around her, but she was well enough, she decided, to be hospitable.

Marie-Christine arrived in the late afternoon with her characteristic way of filling a room — not by being loud, she was rarely loud, but by being entirely herself in it, all attention and energy and the particular warmth she had that felt like a form of weather.

Isabelle kissed her hands. I am well, she said. I have coughed again. These were the facts.

gap_scenes.title: Quarantine
gap_scenes.text:
The word measles arrived at the table the same way all bad news arrived at court tables: behind someone else's news, wrapped in the official language of medical reports, preceded by the kind of careful circumlocution that made it sound almost administrative.

Marie-Christine had measles. She was in her apartment. No visitors.

Isabelle received this information at breakfast on the twenty-sixth of March, 1763, and sat with it for a moment without speaking. Around her the ordinary breakfast went on — bread was passed, chocolate was poured, someone said something about the weather — and she participated in it with the surface of herself while the rest of her went somewhere else entirely.

The logic of quarantine was impeccable. She knew this. She had the small person inside her to think of, and contagion did not negotiate, and the whole system of court medicine and court caution existed precisely to prevent the kind of cascade that had taken Jeanne four months ago.

But the knowledge that Marie-Christine was ill and that she could not go to her and that letters would have to serve where presence should have been — this knowledge settled into her chest alongside the cough and made everything slightly worse.

She would write every day. She would write twice a day if she could. She would console herself in idea, as she always did, though she wrote to Marie-Christine that such consolation was not worth a moment of reality.

She counted the days until Easter, which was April the third, and calculated how long the quarantine would last, and wrote the first of what would become many letters across a distance she could measure in steps.

gap_scenes.title: Writing Across the Distance of a Corridor
gap_scenes.text:
The distances were absurd, that was the thing. She was not far. In an ordinary life, in a city, in a house of reasonable proportions, the space between them would have taken four minutes to cross. But the Hofburg was not a house of reasonable proportions, and the protocols of infection made four minutes an insurmountable distance, and so they wrote.

Isabelle had written seven letters in six days. This was not unusual for her in periods of difficulty — the pen was the instrument through which she thought, and thinking required an audience, and the audience was Marie-Christine, always — but there was a particular urgency to these letters that the others had not quite had. She was not performing tenderness. She was insisting on it. Pushing it through the wall between them by force of language.

Madame d'Erdédy, who had been at her apartment that afternoon, reported that the mood among the ladies of Marie-Christine's household was various: some cheerful, some worried, some merely tired of confinement. Isabelle thanked her for the information and went back to her letter.

I am sorry for the time I will have to spend without seeing you. She had written this in several different formulations over the past week and it was still true and still insufficient. The feeling was larger than the sentence. The feeling had no adequate sentence.

She counted: eight more days, if the doctors were right, until the quarantine would lift. Eight days was not so many. She wrote it at the bottom of the letter as though adding a figure to a sum, and then she sealed it, and then she said to herself: eight days.

gap_scenes.title: Counting Hours Toward Easter
gap_scenes.text:
Easter Sunday was April the third, which meant that Lent had its own momentum, its own calendar of obligations, and Isabelle had attended more church this week than she had in the equivalent period of any previous year, partly from genuine devotion and partly from the recognition that a woman seen regularly at prayer could not be accused of insufficiency of faith, and partly — she admitted this only to herself — because the physical routine of it gave the long days a shape they might otherwise have lacked.

She prayed for Marie-Christine. She prayed for her own health, which continued to be unreliable in ways she continued to underreport. She prayed for the small presence within her that she thought about with a fierce and private attention she shared with no one.

The days without seeing Marie-Christine had accumulated to a number she found intolerable in a way that she recognized as disproportionate and could not modify. She had her daughter to visit — small Teresa, who at ten months was developing the gravity and the watchfulness that Isabelle recognized as her own — and this was consoling in its ordinary way. But it was not the same.

I count the days, the hours, and the minutes, she wrote. This was not an exaggeration. She was embarrassed by the precision of her own feeling, by the fact that she had, in fact, counted, and that the counting had made her feel both better and more ridiculous.

She would see her again soon. She held this fact like a stone in her hand — solid, cool, undeniable.

gap_scenes.title: Impatience
gap_scenes.text:
The first of April, and still the quarantine, and Isabelle woke in a mood she could only describe to herself as a dog's mood: unreasonable, restless, inclined to bite at small things.

She had slept poorly. Her chest was disagreeable. The morning had started with a small ceremony she had been required to attend, standing in the correct arrangement with the correct expression, and she had managed it — she always managed it — but the effort had left her emptied out and irritable.

The news from Marie-Christine's apartments was that she was doing better, was less badly, which was the qualified optimism of people who had learned not to commit themselves too fully. The Empress had reportedly said she was only scratching herself aus Zeitlang — out of boredom — which was the Empress's way of indicating that the crisis had passed but that she reserved the right to worry.

Isabelle sent a note to ask after her news with more eagerness than the formality of a note could properly convey. She was not lazy, she wrote; she had simply not written because she needed the answer before she could say the next thing, and the answer depended on how Marie-Christine was, which she did not know, which was the whole problem.

She spent the afternoon with her books, which normally consoled her, and then with her harpsichord, which consoled her better, and then with nothing at all, simply sitting in the window with the April sun on her face, trying to be patient, which had never been among her stronger capabilities.

gap_scenes.title: The Kammerfrau at the Door
gap_scenes.text:
She had gone to the garden after supper — briefly, just to the nearer garden, the one with the old hornbeam hedge that smelled of wet earth in April — and on her way back she had seen someone entering the courtyard near Marie-Christine's apartments, moving quickly, and for a moment her heart had moved toward her feet.

It was only the Kammerfrau. The Ceintray, who had been at the door with a key and had apparently seen someone coming and had bolted, which struck Isabelle in retrospect as the most absurd and human tableau the whole quarantine had produced.

She went back to her rooms and sat down and felt the adrenaline settle slowly back into ordinary circulation. The garden had been good. The cold April air had been good. The hornbeam was good.

Marie-Christine's health continued to improve, according to the messages that arrived in the morning and the evening. The Empress had called it satisfactory. The Empress's satisfaction was a kind of certification.

Isabelle wrote to tell her she had been wrong to worry, which she had been, and that she had been unable to help it, which was also true. She wrote about the garden and about the late supper and about the hornbeam, all of which were proxies for what she actually wanted to say, which was: two more days, and I can come to you, and the separation will be over, and I will be able to see your face, and I require nothing else from the world on the day that becomes possible.

gap_scenes.title: The Convalescence
gap_scenes.text:
The Empress had given Isabelle a task, which was both a compliment and a form of supervision, and which she accepted in the spirit it was offered — that is, with gratitude and with the quiet satisfaction of someone who has been assigned the only duty she would have chosen freely.

She was to oversee the convalescence. To see to it that Marie-Christine rested, ate adequately, did not immediately return to the full weight of court obligations that her sense of duty would otherwise have pulled her toward. This was a task that required presence, which was to say it required Isabelle to be in her rooms, beside her, at the hours when the day grew long and the patience for invalidity grew thin.

She took this responsibility with absolute seriousness. She appeared every morning. She monitored. She reported to the Empress with the objectivity of someone who had constructed an elaborate personal interest in the subject and was managing to sound professional.

But in the afternoons, when the light came through Marie-Christine's windows in long yellow blocks and the household quieted around them, she sat beside her and they talked or did not talk, and she felt something in herself that she only felt in this proximity — a settling, as though the constant motion of her mind had found a point to turn around.

This is my only consolation, she thought, without which I would die. She had written that somewhere in the letters of the last weeks. She had meant it as hyperbole. In the afternoon light she was less sure it was.

gap_scenes.title: After the Archduke's Departure
gap_scenes.text:
Joseph had left before seven, and the apartment afterward had a particular quality of absence that differed from ordinary quietness — a negative shape where someone had been, the dent in the arrangements of the day left by a person who has recently occupied them.

Isabelle prayed. She went to mass with the household and then back to her apartment, where she prayed again more privately, addressing herself to the Virgin with a directness she could not have managed in the formal liturgy — a conversation between women, she sometimes thought, that cut across the usual protocol.

For sorrows one must seek the quickest consolation, she wrote. The quickest consolation was Marie-Christine, who was somewhere in the palace this morning, alive and recovering and present, and toward whom Isabelle's whole attention turned the way a plant turned toward a window.

But she was not going to prostrate herself at her feet this morning. There was a convent to attend — the hour and a half of community prayer that duty required and which she would endure with the patience of someone performing an obligation they have accepted without pretending to enjoy.

She wrote the letter quickly, in that half-awake state she had before she was fully upright, the words coming from somewhere below the careful surface of herself. She wrote: I am dying of love for you, which was the thing she always said in these letters, the phrase that had become both declaration and signature, both absolutely true and, by repetition, almost ordinary.

Almost. Not quite.

gap_scenes.title: Work Before Noon
gap_scenes.text:
The headache had been bad yesterday, and then very bad, and then the Empress had come to her room in the evening while she was already in bed, which had produced a quality of awkwardness that Isabelle managed by turning it into a private comedy she was already composing for the next letter.

The Augustinians would have appreciated the visit, she thought. She would write that it had been worth six high masses.

This morning the headache was small and retreating, a ghost of yesterday's pain. She had slept well, better than she had expected. She sat at her writing table in the early light and worked — the notebook, the chapter she was always working on, the perpetual project she carried through illness and health and whatever category the days between them occupied.

The Empress had forbidden her the column, whatever social obligation that implied, and she was not entirely displeased. The apartment in April was pleasant when she was alone in it. The light that came through the eastern windows in the morning was clear and a little cold, not yet summer's warmth, still holding the reserve of the long winter.

She wrote to Marie-Christine: do you want to know how I am doing? I would tell you wonderfully, of course. This was not quite true — the headache still moved at the edges of her vision — but it was true enough. She was working. She was alive and working and intending to come to her rooms during the afternoon when the Empress went to her three o'clock engagement.

If I have, she wrote, and did not finish the sentence, and folded the letter and sent it anyway.

gap_scenes.title: The Erdody's Absence
gap_scenes.text:
The Countess Erdody had been gone for three days now, and the gap she left was not precisely her absence — Isabelle was fond of her without being dependent on her in any essential way — but rather what the absence revealed about the shape of her days.

She had been using the time to write to her. Long letters, the kind that required the leisure and the mood that concentrated correspondence demanded. She had explained this to Marie-Christine without much apology: until the Erdody returns, expect only short notes. I am occupied with my long letters elsewhere.

This was true and also a test, she admitted to herself, of the particular variety she could not quite stop administering. She wanted to see what Marie-Christine's reaction would be to this minor reassignment of attention, whether she would mind or not mind or pretend not to mind. She watched for the evidence in the reply.

The reply, when it came, was cheerful and slightly aggrieved in the way that meant she minded. This gave Isabelle a satisfaction she was not particularly proud of.

The spring was advanced now, warm enough in the afternoons that the windows could be opened, and the city sounds entered the apartment — carts on stone, bells, the periodic noise of the guard changing. She was well, all things considered. Better than she had been in March. But she found she was often inexplicably unhappy with Marie-Christine for reasons she could never precisely articulate, and the unhappiness was its own form of devotion.

I kiss you although very unhappy with you. She had written that. She had meant it as tenderly as anything she had ever set down.

gap_scenes.title: The Rival
gap_scenes.text:
There was always someone. This was the operating principle of court life and of Isabelle's inner life both: there was always someone who commanded Marie-Christine's attention in the moment Isabelle wanted it entirely, and the someone was rarely a threat in any real sense but was always present, always requiring their proportion of the time and the smiles and the particular regard that Isabelle had come to think of, with a possessiveness she knew was unreasonable, as belonging in some primary way to herself.

Today the rival was Archduchess Marie-Anne — the learned one, the family's scholar, the woman who had a claim on Marie-Christine through the simple fact of sisterhood that Isabelle could not compete with and could not help resenting slightly.

She sat with this resentment in the way she sat with all her feelings, examining it with a combination of amusement and candor. It was absurd. Marie-Anne was her sister-in-law and entirely inoffensive. The feeling that Marie-Christine's attention was a finite resource and that any quantity of it directed elsewhere constituted a loss was not a feeling that would survive scrutiny.

And yet here she was, at the feet of what she adored, composing a letter in which she would attempt to maneuver Marie-Christine away from her rival by the simple expedient of pointing out that the Archduke was gone and there was no reason therefore not to come.

The morning was gentle and bright. She thought: crazy or wise, sick or healthy, I am always the same when it comes to you. She wrote it down as soon as she thought it, because it was true and because truth this precise was worth keeping.

gap_scenes.title: The Tooth and the Table
gap_scenes.text:
Marie-Christine had a toothache, which she had apparently dealt with in the way she dealt with many inconveniences — by not mentioning it clearly until it had become serious, and then mentioning it in a way that suggested she expected it to resolve itself without intervention.

Isabelle had opinions about teeth. This was not among the subjects on which she had expected to develop strong views, but two years of court medicine and the observation of human suffering in its minor registers had given her a practical education she was willing to deploy.

Do not have it sealed before the inflammation clears, she wrote with more authority than the situation strictly warranted. She had seen teeth just as bad and just as sensitive become manageable with the right approach and survive for years afterward. The gasoline treatment had to be evaluated first. These were the facts.

She was also, in the same afternoon, attending to the matter of a table she had promised — or had been asked about — or had perhaps promised in a letter she could no longer locate precisely. The table existed; it was a matter of arranging its delivery at the right moment in a way that felt like a gift rather than a completion of an obligation.

She was getting dressed for the Saurau, which she would attend because it was on the calendar and one attended things on the calendar, and because she was well enough today, and because the Saurau had good fires and adequate music and the company was not worse than average.

She sealed the letter. It contained, in equal parts, medical advice and love.

gap_scenes.title: Forty Interruptions
gap_scenes.text:
She had woken — she had counted, with the grim precision of the insomniac — more than forty times. Each time she had surfaced enough to know she was awake and then descended again without being entirely sure she had slept. By seven o'clock she had given up and gotten up, and was now sitting at her window in a condition of exhausted irony, watching the May light on the courtyard.

Her fear had apparently passed into the realm of the ordinary, which was what fear did when you lived with it long enough. There had been a moment — she did not dwell on it — when the news from the physicians had suggested the pregnancy might not continue, and the fear had been quite large for several days and then had diminished to its current dimensions, manageable, present, hers.

She thought about the journey to Fischamend, which someone had apparently cancelled or reorganized while she was not paying attention, and the cancellation had affected her in a way entirely disproportionate to the event — a sudden drop in spirits, as though someone had told her winter was returning.

She would write to Marie-Christine about this in the tone she used for dramatic overstatement: I don't know how I didn't die when I found out. She would say she had been preparing herself for death, which she had, in the faint metaphorical sense in which she was always preparing herself for death, as a form of philosophical housekeeping.

This morning, though, she was simply tired and alive, both of these things with great intensity, and the table for Marie-Christine was not yet finished, and the Spring went on.

gap_scenes.title: Before the Scolding
gap_scenes.text:
She had been composing the scolding in her head for several days. This was her method with things that required precise delivery — she rehearsed them in silence until the exact tone was available to her, neither too sharp nor too mild, carrying the feeling without the heat of it.

Marie-Christine had done something. She could not now articulate it clearly, which was part of the problem with scoldings: by the time she was ready to deliver one, the original offense had been joined by several subsequent ones and the whole had become a record of her own accumulated frustration rather than a specific complaint.

But she would write it tonight. Good evening, dear Sister, she would begin, and then: do not think that it is to say sweet things that I am writing to you. This was a tone she had used exactly twice before, and both times the result had been swift capitulation from Marie-Christine, which was not the goal — the goal was the conversation, the clearing of the air — but was always satisfying.

The summer was coming in earnest now, the evenings long and warm, the city below the palace windows loud with the confident energy of the solstice approaching. She had been well these weeks, better than she had been since January, and the wellness made her impatient in a new way — impatient for things to be right, to be clear, to be settled into some arrangement she could trust to last.

She took up her pen. Good evening.

gap_scenes.title: Reward and Earthquake
gap_scenes.text:
The table had finally been delivered, and Marie-Christine had apparently slept well, and so the morning had a quality of achieved things about it that Isabelle found privately satisfying.

She had been to Hetzendorf — or was going to Hetzendorf, the journey was either imminent or just completed, time in the summer had a way of blurring its own edges — and the palace outside Vienna was always a different kind of being than the Hofburg, airier, less weighty, less weighted. She breathed differently there.

Then in the small hours between two and three in the morning, the walls had moved. Not violently — it was a tremor rather than a rupture, the kind of event the earth produced to remind you that the solid ground was only temporarily obliging. But she had been awake for it, which meant she had been awake at three o'clock watching the violent wind follow the tremor and the dawn arrive in the disturbing light of disturbed weather, all brassy and strange.

She had eventually gone back to sleep. Now she was writing about it with the animation she brought to everything unusual, describing the beautiful horror of the skewed dawn, the way the light had been frightening in a way that morning light was not supposed to be.

I hope it will rain so that it will be nice tomorrow, she wrote, which was the most practical thing she could say about the situation. She was going to see Marie-Christine. She had told her she was going to see her. The summer was large and warm and she was in it, still, against all the odds of the last eighteen months, still in it, and still here.

gap_scenes.title: At the Rosary
gap_scenes.text:
She had seen her at the rosary, which was one of those occasions that the church calendar made regular and which court life made ambiguous — every glance across the chapel potentially observed, every arrangement of persons in pews potentially commented upon, the devotional and the social wound together so thoroughly that it was sometimes difficult to know which you were performing.

Marie-Christine had been in her usual place, and Isabelle in hers, and the prayer had proceeded with its familiar rhythm, the decades of the rosary marking time with their patient repetition. She had prayed genuinely, which she was able to do in certain moods — genuinely and also, she admitted, with one part of her attention simply resting on the fact of Marie-Christine's presence in the same room.

Afterward she had not yet read the post, which contained something that she read afterward with close attention. It concerned the Vasquez — matters of loyalty and service and the complicated allegiances of a household where multiple principals competed for the same attention — and it required a response that was more careful than her ordinary letters, a response that navigated rather than declared.

She sat with the letter for a long time. The Vasquez was reliable and devoted and was managing a difficult situation with the grace of someone who had more dignity than most of the people she served. Isabelle wanted to say this and also to say something else, something about trust, about the way that women in palaces built their relationships with the tools available to them.

I am only writing to you in the uncertainty, she said finally. But she sent the letter. The uncertainty was honest.

gap_scenes.title: The Long Letter
gap_scenes.text:
She had been meaning to write it since July. Perhaps since before July — since the previous winter, since the year before that, since some moment early in their correspondence when she had felt the approach of a certain kind of letter like weather coming in from the west and had known it was coming and had not yet found the words.

October arrived, and still the letter was not written. She had taken it out in pieces — the idea of it, the intention of it — and set it back down again, telling herself she would write it when she had time, when she was feeling well, when the days were not so full. None of these conditions had been fully satisfied.

Then one morning she sat down and began it with the words: In truth you are too good. She had already been going to destroy what she'd written. She didn't.

The letter became very long. It covered things she had been holding for a long time — her love, which was absolute and required no qualification; her concern for Marie-Christine's soul, which she could not separate from her concern for her happiness; her fear that the death she sometimes spoke of too easily was not so far away after all. She had been carrying this fear privately all autumn, offering it to God in her morning prayers and then putting it in her pocket for the day.

Perhaps we will be separated, she wrote. Perhaps death will end a life which is dear to me only because it is dedicated to you.

She sealed the letter and delivered it herself and did not wait for an answer.

gap_scenes.title: The Painting and the Presentiment
gap_scenes.text:
She had been playing the violin that morning, which was what she did when the words were not available, which happened less often than one might expect but did sometimes happen, particularly in the late autumn when the light contracted and the days had a quality of diminishment about them.

The painting stood on its easel — the child Jesus she was working on, the small figure that kept accumulating associations she had not initially intended. She looked at it from her chair and thought about what it would mean to finish it, and about what she owed Marie-Christine, and about time.

The presentiment had come on quietly, without drama, over the course of two days. Not a sudden certainty but an accumulation, a gathering weight of something she could not name except to say that it did not feel like fear. It felt more like — anointing, perhaps. Like something settling rather than something approaching.

She would die before another year passed. She was not certain of this, was willing to allow that her head might be spinning, but she was also more certain than she was comfortable admitting.

The remarkable thing was how peaceful this felt. Not happy, not willing — but peaceful. A sweetness in the soul that she could not explain and did not try to.

She would tell Marie-Christine. She would tell her everything, as she always had. But she would tell her not to make her seem like a visionary; that part she could do without. The truth was stranger and more private than a vision, and it belonged to them.

gap_scenes.title: Small Griefs
gap_scenes.text:
The news arrived in the mid-afternoon, delivered by one of the household who reported it with the matter-of-fact tone used for information that is inconvenient rather than catastrophic: the Archduke no longer goes out on horseback.

Isabelle received this and was quiet for a moment. It was a small thing. Horses were dangerous, particularly in autumn when the ground was slippery, and the physicians had perhaps recommended it and perhaps his own caution had arrived at the same conclusion. It was a practical decision.

And yet she felt it as a kind of diminishment, as one more small door closing in the architecture of an ordinary life. She had learned in the last months to read these small closings — the adjustments, the accommodations, the ways in which the body began to edit its own ambitions downward — with a literacy she had not had before.

She sat in the midst of this misery, which was the word she used, and it was true and also somewhat performative, and the combination was characteristically her own.

The court was in its autumn rhythm, formal and relentless, the calendar full of obligations that did not pause for private weather. She would appear where she was required to appear. She would be present and gracious and attentive in the approved modes.

But she wrote the note first — brief, dry, not without humor, in the style of someone reporting a small absurdity to the only person who would understand why it mattered — and sent it before the afternoon was over.

gap_scenes.title: What Cannot Be Said Aloud
gap_scenes.text:
There were things she could not say in person. This had always been true of her — she who talked more than anyone, who wrote more than anyone, who produced such a continuous and extravagant record of her own interior life — but it had become more true in recent weeks, as the presentiment had become more constant and the things she needed to say had become larger.

She did not dare speak. This was the word she used: dare. Not could not, but dared not, which was a different thing, which implied that she had the words and the words were too large for the room.

So she sat across from Marie-Christine in the afternoons, or beside her, in the October light that came through the windows at a low angle now, and she was present in the way she had been present for three years — entirely, unreservedly, with that particular quality of attention that she had given to nothing and no one else in her life — and she did not say the largest things.

She wrote them instead, in letters that she folded very small and sent by the most discreet of the household's servants. She wrote: yesterday I spent carefully. This was true. Every day recently she spent carefully, as though days were currency and the supply was being audited.

I kiss you a thousand and a thousand times, she wrote. The repetition was not rhetorical. It was the gesture of someone adding up a sum they do not want to reach the end of.

gap_scenes.title: Archduchess Isabeau
gap_scenes.text:
She had begun referring to herself in the third person in certain of her letters, a habit that had started as a joke — the Archduchess Isabeau, patient sufferer of all ailments — and had grown into something that served her in ways she had not entirely planned.

The third person created a small necessary distance. When she wrote that Archduchess Isabeau would die soon, she was able to look at the sentence as something being said about a character rather than a declaration from within her own chest. The fiction was thin, but it was a fiction, and fictions were useful.

The illness is going to get worse, she wrote, and it goes from bad to worse, and this disease is all the more dangerous because the only means there could be cannot be used. She was speaking of love. She was always, under all the other languages, speaking of love, which was the one disease for which she had no treatment and which she had no wish to cure.

She is dying of love for you, she wrote. Isabeau is dying of love for you. She should still love you, she can't, and I think the best thing would be to tell you when I see you, and then I will be healthy again.

This was her hope, stated in the grammar of a fairy tale. The seeing would heal her. Or it would not, because nothing healed this, but the seeing was the closest she could come to relief, and she would reach for it for as long as she was able to reach for anything.

She sealed the letter. The face is a little sick, she added, but your favorite place is not. She was still capable of that. It mattered.

gap_scenes.title: Advice to Marie
gap_scenes.text:
She was not writing a testament. She had told herself this firmly before she began and she told herself again at intervals as the pages accumulated. This was not the language of someone closing accounts. This was a friendship, still ongoing, still in motion, and what she was writing was counsel from that friendship, from inside it, with full knowledge of all its particulars.

And yet. The candles had burned down twice while she wrote and she had replaced them and continued. The night outside the window was November's night, cold and complete, and she could hear the guards below moving through their prescribed routes with their prescribed regularity, the palace keeping time as it always had.

She was thinking about what Marie-Christine would face after. She did not say after what; it was implicit and she let it be implicit, because to say it directly would have required her to stop writing, and she was not ready to stop. She thought about the Empress, who would grieve and then would make use of that grief in the way she made use of everything — as material, as motivation, as one more thing to survive. She thought about the Archduke, who was not always easy. She thought about Vasquez, who was reliable and steady and worth more than was generally appreciated.

And she thought about Marie-Christine herself, who was impulsive and brilliant and prone to judgment and possessed of more capacity for genuine love than she herself understood. Who needed to be reminded not to speak before she thought and to allow people to believe she was learning things she already knew, and to let herself go completely before those who needed her.

I tried to lead you along a clear path, she wrote. Her hand was steady. Her heart was very full. She kept writing.

letter_reimaginings.text:
Colorno, July 6, 1760.

I held your letter in both hands before I read it. The seal was already broken — some courier had been clumsy, or careless — but still I paused, feeling the weight of the paper, the faint residue of your touch on its surface. A letter from Marie-Christine. My sister-in-law whom I have never yet met, and yet whom I have already begun, in some wordless animal way, to need.

When I finally read it, I stood at the window in the morning light and I confess I trembled. Not from cold. The Italian summer is merciless. I trembled because your friendship — the warmth and directness of it, the way you simply claimed me as yours — reached through all the formal distance between Parma and Vienna and took hold of something in my chest.

You are right to demand my friendship. It belongs to you. That is what I said and what I meant, and I mean it now more than when I wrote it, having read your words a second and a third time and found new depths of kindness in them each time.

How does one explain a feeling that has no proper name? The tie that draws me to you is not merely duty, though duty is present. It is not merely the bond of those who will soon be family, though that bond is real. It is something prior to all of that — something I recognized the moment I read your first words, as though I had been waiting without knowing I was waiting.

I wanted you to know: my feelings for you are stronger than any eloquence I possess. I could write for a month and still fall short of the whole extent of it. So I will only say that when you come to know me — as you will, soon, when I arrive in Vienna and we stand in the same room for the first time — you will see it in my face before I can speak a word. I am already yours, dear sister. I am already, without having seen you, entirely and faithfully yours.

Colorno, July 26, 1760.

Your letters arrive like the news of victories, and like victories they make my blood quicken and my heart expand with something I am still learning to name.

Two letters now. Each one bringing triumph in its wake — first the news of Laudon's victory over the Prussians, and now another. I am beginning to believe there is something charmed about the conjunction of your handwriting and good fortune. I find myself thinking: let the third letter bring the final defeat of the Prussian king, let it bring us peace, let it bring me to you sooner.

But the war is not what occupies my heart when I read you. What occupies my heart is you. The way you speak of yourself with too little esteem, as though your worth were a question still open. I want to argue with you about this the moment I can speak to you in person. You deserve better from yourself than you give.

You say my qualities do not deserve the warmth you have shown me. You are gracious in this error and I will not entirely correct you — I have too many faults, as you will discover — but I insist that my tenderness for you deserves every atom of what you have offered. My tenderness is real. It is present, as you say my friendship is past, present and future: it will not diminish with time or proximity or the inevitable disappointments of knowing me as I actually am.

I am a good Austrian, you wrote to tell me. I am that and more. I am yours. Consider it: the girl raised in Italy, arriving in Vienna in autumn, already belonging to this family in her heart before she belongs to it in law. Already, without having seen your face, entirely convinced that you are one of the finest people alive.

Write to me again. The weeks until October stretch before me like a sentence.

Parma, August 26, 1760.

Five more weeks. I count them the way one counts the last days of an illness — with impatience that is almost its own pain.

Something has been happening here in Parma that I find I need to confess to you. The Germans have begun to arrive, the advance party of the world I am moving toward, and each time I see one of them in the street or at court, I feel a warmth that surprises me. I love the German nation — I said it and I believe it, not merely because gratitude requires me to, not merely because I am about to be counted one of them. The feeling is prior to duty. It is natural to me, as natural as the pull I feel toward you, toward that family, toward that cold northern city I have never seen but already dream of as home.

I suspect, if I am honest, that these two loves are not entirely separate. That part of what draws me toward Vienna, toward Austria, toward the German tongue and character, is the fact that you are there. That you wait there. That I will soon be in the same building, the same rooms, breathing the same cold Viennese air.

I am writing to you half-asleep. I managed only five hours last night and yesterday was long and wearing, and I am aware that my words are wandering, losing their direction. Forgive me. When I am tired, my heart speaks more directly than my mind would wish, and what it says is only this:

I am coming to you. I am coming as fast as the weeks will carry me. I embrace you with my whole soul — not as a formality, not as one completes a letter, but as a fact of my interior life that I cannot suppress and no longer wish to.

Five weeks. I can survive five weeks.

Vienna, October-November 1760.

Do not play the harpsichord beautifully tonight. I am begging you. Play it badly, miss the notes, let the instrument be unpleasant — because if you play as you played yesterday, I will expire at your feet from something that has no decorous name in any language I have been taught.

I wrote that and I let it stand. Because it is true, and because I have discovered, since coming to Vienna, that truth with you is the only thing worth practicing.

I am dying of love for you. I write the words and they do not feel excessive; they feel like a plain and careful account of my present condition. Dying — yes, that is the word — not because I suffer, but because the self I was before you seems, in retrospect, an incomplete thing, a sketch that is only now being filled in. When you played last night, something in me that had been held tightly open.

The harpsichord was always an instrument I could take or leave. Now it is unbearable to me, because it carries your hands, your concentration, the slight tilt of your head when you are listening to what you have made. If the harpsichord were unpleasant to me, I might be safe. It is not unpleasant. Nothing associated with you is unpleasant. This is my predicament.

So let me live. Let me adore you at a safe distance — or, failing that, let me adore you without distance at all, which is also, in its way, a form of surviving. My friendship is past, present, and future, as I wrote to you in summer when friendship was all I dared to call it. The word now feels both true and insufficient.

Write me back. Tell me what to call this. Or say nothing, and simply play badly tonight.

Vienna, October-November 1760.

Thank you for letting me see the concert. The words are simple and I mean them completely.

I have been thinking since this morning about what it means to be let in — to be given admission to something another person holds private. You share your music with many, yes, your performances are public affairs with all the ceremony the court demands, all the eyes and the applause and the prescribed admiration. But you let me see something different last night. The way you hear music before you play it, the interior silence that comes over you in the moments before your hands move — that was not for the room. That was for me, because you had let me see it, because you had made room for me beside you in a way that the other onlookers were not.

On the first day, I told you, I will make you something in return. I meant it as an exchange, a gift of equal weight. Now I am less certain. What I can make for you — what I can offer in return for the way your music passes through me and rearranges everything it touches — may take longer than a single morning to assemble.

I am learning, since coming to Vienna, that I have more to learn than I had thought. I arrived believing myself reasonably educated, reasonably formed, reasonably prepared for the world I was entering. Your harpsichord has disabused me of this. Your playing has shown me that there are registers of experience I have not yet reached, and that the path to them runs, at present, entirely through you.

So: thank you for the concert. On the first day, I will make you something. I hope it will be worthy of what you gave me.

Vienna, late 1760.

I am going to Saint-Etienne and I resent every step of the distance it will put between us.

You know what I mean. I will not say it in plain words — I have already said it once today and even I have some sense of what is permissible — but you know. The afternoon was an opportunity, the kind that appears rarely and vanishes if not taken, and Saint-Etienne is consuming it, and I am going there with great reluctance, with a feeling in my body like something unfinished.

I will try to come to your rooms for a moment before I am obliged to leave. I don't know yet when. The schedule is not entirely my own. But I want you to know that the effort will be made, that I will look for the gap in the afternoon's arrangements, that I am not resigned to this separation.

I am in a foul mood, if I am honest — the mood of a dog kept from what it wants by a fence whose logic it cannot understand. I slept a great deal and am otherwise well in body. The mood is entirely of the heart's making.

I kiss you in thought with all my might. This is not a convention. When I write it, I am imagining your face — exactly your face, the particular quality of your attention when it turns toward me — and pressing my lips against the image of it with a force that would startle you if it were real and not imagined.

Might you be free when I return? I will come straight to you if the evening permits.

Vienna, October-November 1760.

La Christiani is too sensible to make such a blunder, and I am glad the Archduke had the good judgment to conduct himself with propriety. But this is not what I am writing to tell you.

I am writing to tell you this: you are owed more than you are given. If he knew everything he owes you — the steadiness of your character, the quality of your mind, the way you make every room you enter more honest merely by being present in it — he would spend his days in a different attitude entirely. He would be grateful in a way that is presently beyond him.

I think about this often: the distance between what you deserve and what is offered you. It makes something in me restless, even angry — a feeling I have no right to, perhaps, but which exists nonetheless. You are patient with circumstances that I would find intolerable. You move through this court with a grace I could never replicate, absorbing its demands, its surveillance, its endless requirement that you be pleasing and available and never too much of anything.

And then there is this: you are too much. You are too alive, too acute, too capable of real friendship for this place to hold comfortably. The court cannot quite contain you. I see this in the way people respond to you — with admiration they don't entirely understand, with a slight wariness in the faces of those who sense that you see through them.

I see through none of it. I see only you, exactly as you are, and what I see leaves me with no words equal to the seeing.

If he knew everything he owes you. But I think I do, or am beginning to. And I intend to pay it.

Vienna, early December 1760.

You treacherous, wonderful creature. You told the Empress.

I am writing to you with something between outrage and laughter, and I cannot fully commit to either because underneath both is a warmth I did not intend to feel so openly this morning. The Empress wrote to thank me for the Saint Nicholas gift, and in her letter it was clear that she knew I had been informed of your involvement — your beautiful, complicated, entirely characteristic involvement — and I was caught absolutely off guard.

So tell me: did you confess? Did you go to her willingly and admit the whole scheme, or did she draw it out of you? I need to know how much to reproach you. If you went of your own initiative, the reproach will be sharp but brief. If she extracted it from you, I may forgive you entirely, because in that case you simply proved, once again, that you cannot dissemble under her gaze, and I find that particular quality of yours almost unbearably endearing.

You have no secrets from her. I have observed this. When the Empress turns that careful attention of hers toward you, something in your face shifts — not fear, not quite guilt, but a transparency that you cannot prevent and that she reads without effort. It makes you both more vulnerable and more trustworthy than almost anyone else at this court.

I, however, have secrets. Most of them concern you. I am not certain she cannot read those too, when she looks at me with something knowing in her expression and asks how I am settling in.

I am settling in, I tell her. Very well, I say. And I mean it in every way, and in some ways more than she intends to ask.

Vienna, December 1760.

You are, of all creatures in creation, the most insufferable. I say this with great tenderness and a complete lack of success at maintaining any severity whatsoever.

Your curling animals — those instruments of elaborate personal torment that you somehow believe constitute a reasonable thing to impose on another person — came for me again this morning. I sat through it. I sat through the whole ordeal because I wanted to be there, because I had been looking forward to being in your rooms, and because I am apparently willing to endure a great deal for the privilege of your proximity.

But listen: I felt the most extraordinary sensation come over me while I was in that chair, in that warm room, with you moving around me. Not from the curling irons — nothing so romantic. Something came over me from inside, a sudden wave of disorientation that I had to manage quietly by sitting very still and gripping the arm of the chair. I did not want you to see it. I did not want you to worry, or to stop, or to look at me with that particular expression of yours that would have undone me entirely.

I am writing this as my justification, so that if I am ever found to have died of a sudden spell while sitting in your company, you will know it was not suicide and not your fault. It was, rather, the accumulated weight of being near you, which presses on my chest in a way that is not entirely unpleasant but is not, medically speaking, sustainable as a permanent condition.

I kiss you. Gently, this morning. My constitution requires it.

Vienna, December 1760.

I could not write to you earlier, and this is why: I rose late, having been unable to sleep before the small hours, lying in the dark with the city quiet outside and my mind refusing its rest. When I finally woke it was to the obligation of writing to the Empress — a duty that could not be deferred, a debt of thanks for the grace she extended to me, which I tried to express with the dignity she deserves and which I fear I expressed only partially.

And then I wanted to write to you. I have been wanting to write to you, in fact, since the previous evening, since we last spoke and since something you said — in passing, I think you meant it as nothing — stayed with me through the whole of the night and is still present in my thoughts now, in the mid-morning, with the cold December light coming through the window and the court busy somewhere beyond my door.

I slept a little better last night. I note this for you because you asked about my health yesterday with a genuine worry in your face that I noticed and that I want to answer properly. I am all right. I am tired in a way that is not entirely physical, a tiredness of the adjustment — of being new here, of learning everything at once, of wanting so much so immediately and not knowing how to be patient about it.

You are what I am impatient for, primarily. The brief and formal moments we manage in the full glare of the court are never sufficient. I want the long afternoon, the candlelit hour, the conversation that does not have to end because someone is watching.

Soon, perhaps. Forgive the short note. I had to write to the Empress first.

Vienna, end of December 1760.

Here are my pearls. You asked for them and I give them without hesitation and with only a little of the pang that comes with parting from a thing that has been close to one's throat.

They are good pearls. They came with me from Parma, chosen by my mother — or perhaps by someone my mother trusted, I am not certain — and I have worn them on occasions of ceremony and occasions of pleasure, and once, I recall, on an evening when I wore nothing else of consequence and I sat alone reading by the fire and felt, for an hour, entirely content with my own company. They carry that memory. I give it to you with them.

Tell me how we are dining tonight. Tell me if you still intend to speak to me as you said yesterday — because yesterday you promised something that I have been turning over in my mind all day, something about what you wanted to say and when you might say it. I have been very patient. I have been, I think, remarkably composed given that you left me waiting with nothing but the shape of an intention and no content.

Today is also, though I am aware it sounds self-interested to mention it, the last day of the year. My last day as nineteen. Tomorrow I will be twenty and the court will celebrate and I will smile and receive well-wishes and I will be looking, across whatever room we are assembled in, for your face, for the particular quality of your regard when it falls on me, for the private signal beneath the public occasion that tells me you are here and that this matters.

The pearls are yours. I am, in some ways that I cannot yet fully articulate, also yours. Tell me how we are dining.

Vienna, January 1, 1761.

Good evening, my sister. The New Year has arrived and I am writing to you by candlelight with your note still in my hand, having read it twice and found in it more layers than its surface suggests.

This prelate you ask about — yes, I know him, and he is indeed among my friends, and yes he adores you, it is obvious to anyone with functioning eyes. I would be more scandalized by what you inferred from the stamp if I were not so aware of my own glass walls on this subject. I will reproach you very gently and then let the matter rest.

What I want to say, and what I find I can say more freely by candlelight on the first night of a new year than I can say in the ordinary arrangements of our days, is this: I would be sorry if all my letters reached you. I have written things to you that I would not wish to exist in the public record of my life. Not because they are shameful — I do not believe they are shameful — but because they are mine, and they are yours, and the space between us in which they live is the most private and necessary space I have yet found in this city that is not yet home.

I will eat if I can, I will sleep — deeply, I hope, for the first time in some days — and I will love you. That is the plain account of my immediate future. I will love you constantly, as I have been doing since before I understood what I was doing, and I will do so without apology and without the performance of a feeling I do not have.

Happy New Year, my Christine. I kiss you with my whole heart.

Vienna, between December 26 and January 18, 1761.

Brother Charles had a better night.

I am writing to you before I write to anyone else, before the morning's full weight of obligation descends, because I wanted you to have this first. Not because it is the most important news in the household — the Empress will have it through her own channels before I finish this sentence — but because giving you the first news is a habit I seem to have formed without deciding to form it. When something happens, my first movement is toward you.

I noticed this sometime in November, this reflex. The impulse to turn in your direction before I have decided to turn anywhere. I dismissed it then as the understandable attachment of a newcomer to the one person who has been consistently kind. But I am less certain of that explanation now. Kindness is not sufficient to account for the way your presence reorganizes my thoughts, the way your absence from a room makes the room feel like a problem to be solved.

Brother Charles had a better night. The smallpox is terrible; we are all afraid, and the Empress is carrying a grief in her face that I cannot look at directly without feeling something collapse in my own chest. But he is better than yesterday, and I could not wait to tell you.

I did not want to fail to give you the first news. Happy, if this small report can convince you of how much I love you. That is a strange thing to write — to use a brother's illness as evidence of feeling. But perhaps it is true that we reveal ourselves most precisely in what we reach for when we are frightened.

Vienna, between December 26, 1760 and January 18, 1761.

I am beginning, at last, to hope.

Brother Charles had a good night. It should, they tell us, have been a night of crisis — the disease moves through its phases with a terrible predictability, and this was to have been among the worst — but it was not as bad as feared. We held our breath through the dark hours and this morning the breath released.

I have been drawing his portrait these past days. It is something I do when I cannot do anything useful — when waiting is the only available action and waiting is not enough. I take up my pencils and I try to fix someone I love in a form that the disease cannot touch. I made two of him yesterday, between one visit and the next, and I am sending them both to you because there is nowhere else I want them to be.

You will see that my hand was not entirely steady. The fear gets into the lines. But the likeness is there, I think. The particular quality of his face, which is a young man's face still, which should have many years left in it. I am asking the portrait to stand in for confidence I do not yet fully feel.

The night was better than the previous one. We are constantly afraid, but we are also, this morning, cautiously alive in our hope. I wanted you to know. I wanted you to have the portraits and the careful, fragile news of improvement, and to know that in the middle of all this fear, my first movement is still toward you.

Farewell. Watch over yourself in these cold weeks. I could not bear any other losses.

Vienna, January 1761.

Here is the almanac I promised you. Look at it carefully — it deserves your attention, and I am angry, I find, at the engraving that represents the subject of marriage, because I searched through it for you and could not find your face there. You ought to be in it. The person of greatest relevance to the institution, as I understand it privately, is you.

Last night I thought about death again. This is not a new habit — I have been thinking about death, in a philosophical rather than a despairing way, since I was quite young and began to find the question genuinely interesting. But last night the thought took on a particular color that surprised me: I do not want to die because dying means separation from you, and I am convinced, with the serene certainty of someone who has examined the evidence carefully, that no one else in the world could offer you the quality of friendship I offer.

This is not vanity. It is an observation about specificity. What I have with you is not something I carried with me from Parma that could be redirected toward another person. It is made of us — of the particular overlap of how I think and how you think, of the things we both find funny and the things we both find unbearable, of the way your mind moves and the way I am constituted to follow it. Another person might love you more wisely or more beautifully. None would love you in precisely this way.

So I intend to live. And I intend to see you this morning if the afternoon's arrangements can be managed, and I intend to kiss you and kiss you with all my heart, and I intend to tell you that the separation of death is not a thing I can contemplate with equanimity.

Farewell, my adorable sister. Our plans are disrupted and I am beside myself about it. But I kiss you, again and again.

Vienna, February 1761.

I came to your house this morning in great haste, in the gap between one obligation and the next, hoping we might have a moment that was ours.

You were not cruel enough to refuse me your hair. I am noting this because I want you to understand what that means to me — not the physical fact of it, though the physical fact of it is not nothing — but the permission it represents. The willingness to be touched, casually, without the full ceremony of court presentation, in the ordinary intimacy of a morning. I think about that permission a great deal.

For my part I have been managing tolerably until now, though my devotions today failed to produce the peace they are supposed to produce. I am all — I am entirely, completely, helplessly krantig, which is a word I have begun to use because the German seems to carry more weight than the French equivalent, though perhaps it is only that it sounds like what it describes, a hardness and a persistence, a state that will not be resolved by prescription.

I saw my sisters this morning at their devotions — Jeanne and Josépha both. I will not tell you what I thought of Josépha's expression during communion except that I have never in my life witnessed anything quite like it, and that I will save the full account for when I see you in person, because it requires performance to be properly conveyed.

I am coming to you as soon as I can manage it. Wait for me. I kiss you with all my strength while I wait for the moment I can be in the same room as you again, which is where I am most fully myself, and which I notice I require now more than I require most other things.

Vienna, February 1761.

Dear Alte. My old one. My particular, impossible, singular friend.

I had not intended to write to you. I was going to be sensible about this morning and let the post go without adding to it, because what I have to say does not entirely fit into the genre of letters as I was taught to write them. But your note arrived — wildly, delightfully, impossibly — and I find I cannot not respond to it, because you are right that there is nothing stronger in the world than what exists between us, and right also that this very strength is what makes my head spin.

I blame myself for your cough. You were in my rooms last night until late — later than is wise, later than can be explained innocently to anyone who might have noticed the hour — and the cold came in through the window I had opened because I was too warm, and I suspect the cold found you, and now you are coughing, and I am sorry, and I also cannot bring myself to wish the evening different in any particular.

There was a priest, they say, who went mad because he heard a voice in his ear that cried for vengeance and gave him no rest. I had a voice last night that gave me no sleep either, though it was not crying for vengeance. I will tell you what it was crying for when I see you. It is not the kind of thing that goes in writing.

In any case, my particular madness is simply this: I love you. That is the whole of it. The madness is the love and the love is the madness and I have stopped trying to distinguish between them.

I will be at your house at ten for dinner. Order what you want, wherever you want, and I will be there. I kiss you.

Vienna, February 3, 1761.

The last day of carnival. An occasion, they tell me, for giving oneself pleasures. The only pleasure I want is to speak to you, so here I am, pen in hand, before you can even fully read my first note of the morning.

I adore you. I want to begin with that, without qualification or preamble, simply as a statement of fact that the carnival season and the abundance of masked and costumed strangers and the whole ridiculous festivity of the court cannot touch or diminish. I adore you.

Having said that: I must confess something. At last night's ball, I was briefly, temporarily, and entirely laughingly unfaithful to you. I entered the room and there was a young woman — described by her companions, apparently, as beautiful as Venus — and I looked, because I look at beautiful things, and then I looked again, and then I examined, with the attentiveness of a naturalist, what exactly was before me.

She had features and beauty and graces, they had said. The reality: she was approximately the height of a small pig, with a mouth of notable width and a nose that announced its owner's intelligence with, shall we say, considerable force. I was enchanted for approximately three minutes. The enchantment was sincere but brief. It lasted precisely until the moment I remembered your face, which is a face that does not lose comparison with anything the carnival might produce.

You prevail. You always prevail. This is the thing about you that I have stopped being surprised by and started simply accepting as a feature of my landscape: whatever and whoever else I encounter, you remain the standard against which everything is measured, and nothing yet has come close to the measure.

Farewell, my dear rival-of-all-rivals. I am yours today as on every day.

Vienna, February-March 1761.

I love you, divinity — you who make the jealous despair and the devoted tremble. It is a pity you do not sing French.
