I have been imagining it: your voice in an opera, some pastoral thing, Laurette and Zerbin perhaps, the innocent comedy of love in an idealized landscape. You would be magnificent. The thought of it is almost a grief, that this version of you does not publicly exist.

But I am uncertain whether I should name you Venus or something more complicated. Venus is all sweetness and you are not always sweet — you have a jealousy in you that flares like a struck flint, sudden and bright, and I am never entirely sure whether I find it alarming or whether I find it, in the privacy of my interior life, something quite else.

Here is my advice, which you did not ask for: let them compete for you. Let whoever wishes to compete, compete. Do not choose one divinity over another. Come instead and surrender yourself to the only one I have ever recognized as real — sweet indifference, the goddess of genuine contentment, the happiness that asks nothing of circumstances because it is made of something more interior than circumstances can reach.

I have nothing to do at home. I have been in my rooms for an hour with nothing necessary in front of me, thinking about you, which is my primary occupation when I am not being required to be occupied by something else. Come and tell me when you want me. I am at your orders from this moment on. It is only the fear of inconveniencing you that has kept me from climbing your staircase already.

I love you. I am coming up the moment you give the word.

Vienna, February-March 1761.

Hello, adorable sister. Good morning from my side of the corridor.

I have been awake since early and thinking about you, which is my customary way of beginning a day now — a fact I have stopped being startled by and begun to think of as simply my life. I think about you in the morning before anything else intrudes, and what I think is generally some version of: how is she, is she well, did she sleep as she promised she would sleep, and I want to know the answers before I can properly begin anything.

You promised you would sleep. I am holding you to that promise with the full weight of my concern, which is considerable and which you should not take lightly.

I would like — and here the letter becomes something I might have started with, if I were braver or less accustomed to arriving at the point by a circuitous route — I would like to see you this morning. Not at the formal hour, not in the context of court attendance or family obligation. I would like a genuine morning, the kind we occasionally manage, the kind that consists of your company and a certain amount of mutual ease and the particular quality of conversation that only happens when neither of us is performing.

Tell me if this is possible. Tell me how you are. Tell me that you slept and that your night was quiet and that you woke feeling like yourself.

I am waiting for your word, as always, as perpetually, as hopelessly and happily as a person who has simply accepted that this particular waiting is now the central condition of her existence.

Vienna, March 1761.

For now, cruel sister, I release all thoughts of wickedness.

I had been nursing a resentment. You know me well enough to have expected it — when I am thwarted I withdraw into something sharp and self-contained, something that resembles dignity but is mostly wounded feeling wearing dignity's clothes. I had been preparing, in the privacy of my own rooms, a retaliation of some kind. Nothing dramatic. Simply the cold precision of someone who has been genuinely stung and wants the other person to know it.

And then you made me sweat and cry. Not in the way of cruelty — in the way of the opposite of cruelty, the way that disarms rather than wounds, the way that reaches through the withdrawal and finds the person inside who is not cold at all but very much the reverse. You know exactly how to do this. You know exactly where I am most permeable, where the controlled surface gives way, and you applied your knowledge with the precision of someone who has been studying the architecture of my defenses for months.

It is too much. Making me sweat and cry is too much, when I had been maintaining such excellent and dignified composure. I had been prepared to be withering. You made me incapable of anything withering whatsoever.

So: I give up the wickedness. I surrender it. I am no longer angry, or rather I am angry but the anger has transformed into something so thoroughly mixed with other feelings that it cannot operate independently.

I am at your door this afternoon if you will have me.

Vienna, March 1761.

Hello, adorable sister. You make my head turn.

I have been thinking about something strange this morning: the fact that I imagine you reading this. While I write, I am also elsewhere, standing at your shoulder, watching your eyes move across the lines I am making. Self-esteem is a peculiar ailment — I know this, I acknowledge it freely — and mine manifests in this particular way, in the fantasy that you have already read me, that my words have already reached you and you are already forming a response, that the gap between writing and being read is already, somehow, closed.

This is a fantasy produced by wanting to be known. By you specifically. By the version of being-known that only you provide, which is different from the being-known I receive from anyone else in this court, in this family, in this life I have been assigned and which I am, on better days, genuinely grateful for.

You know me as I actually am. Not the performed version, not the diplomatic bride-of-the-Archduke version with her careful French and her impeccable manners and her excellent posture. The real one. The one who writes to you at all hours and cannot sleep and has opinions about music that she is not supposed to hold quite so strongly and laughs at the wrong moments in ceremony and is, all things considered, rather more herself than the occasion usually requires.

You read me and you are not alarmed. This, I think, is the nearest thing to happiness I have yet encountered in Vienna.

I am waiting to know if you have read this. Tell me immediately.

Vienna, March 1761.

I am here again, too cruel sister, in the particular torment of waiting.

You are reading it now — or you have read it — the thing I sent you this morning, the long letter, the one that took me three attempts and said more than I intended and which I sent before I could reconsider, because reconsidering is a weakness I cannot afford when it comes to telling you the truth. You are holding it or have held it, and you are forming a judgment, and I am on this side of the wall not knowing what the judgment is.

I want to see you. I want to stand before you and explain myself in person, to give you all the interior context that a letter necessarily leaves out, to show you with my face and my voice and the whole of my present self that what I said was not what you might fear it means but what I know it means, which is something that requires presence to properly communicate.

I love you in your nature. I want you to hear that clearly. I love the version of you that actually exists — the complicated, jealous, brilliant, occasionally maddening, entirely irreplaceable reality of you — and the idea of you being anything other than exactly that distresses me past coherence.

My teeth hurt. My head spins. My fever is metaphorical but my love is literal and I intend to carry it out to the letter and deposit it at your feet the moment you tell me I am forgiven.

Farewell. Tell me my fate when you are ready. I still love you with rage.

Vienna, early summer 1761.

You will have only one word from me today, dear sister, because I have just come from confession and there is a stack of other notes demanding to be written, and I am doing very well, and I am beginning to suspect I am growing fat, and none of this is the thing I want to say to you but all of it is true.

The thing I want to say is harder. Confession has left me in an odd state — not purged or lightened as it is supposed to leave one, but reflective, overly conscious of the gap between what one says and what one feels, between the words the confessional requires and the words the heart keeps generating without permission.

I am doing very well. I want you to know that. And I want you to tell me how you are doing, please, in more than the general court currency of 'I am well, thank you.' I want to know specifically — how you slept, what you ate, whether the headache came back, whether the afternoon was long or short and dull or interesting, whether you thought of me at any point and if so when and how.

I am asking for an account of you. The detailed, particular, interior account. Because I am, at this moment, standing in the early-summer morning having just confessed everything I could bring myself to confess, and the thing that sits heaviest in my chest — lighter than a sin, heavier than a sentiment — is simply the wish to know how you are.

Farewell. I kiss you. Please write back immediately.

Vienna, summer 1761.

I know your cruelty too well, dear sister, to imagine you would accept a gift from me directly. So I am not giving it to you. I am giving it to Lisette — the comedy character, your alter ego in the pastoral games we play, the fictional beloved of fictional Linon — and Lisette must accept it from her first lover, because Linon is in good enough condition and his feelings are sufficiently genuine that this is a proper gift for a proper occasion. We are going to be married, after all, in the fiction. This is the wedding present.

But I want to write to you as Zerbin, too, in the character I have been playing in your imagination and mine since the summer began. Zerbin who languishes. Zerbin who loves you with an intensity that would be tragic if it were not also, frankly, ridiculous — this pining, desperate, theatrical lover who cannot close his eyes without seeing your face.

Dear Laurette: was this what you intended for the third day of our fictional marriage? Can you watch, with equanimity, your lover expire at your feet? I am an innocent lover. I did not think I had done anything to offend you. I wait for the judgment you will pronounce, knowing that I am incapable of not loving you and incapable of not telling you so.

Tell me my fault. Let me wash it away. Otherwise know that even in hell, which my dramatic nature assures me awaits the unduly devoted, I will live to love you.

You know my heart too well not to relent. Come back. We will kiss again tomorrow. Mein Engerl, I adore you.

Vienna, summer 1761.

How do I dare appear before you? I am asking this honestly.

I got angry. I will not pretend I did not, or that the anger was measured and appropriate. It came up suddenly, the way the worst things in me come up — from a place below deliberation, faster than good sense — and I said things I would not have said with the longer interval to consider them. I said them in the first movement of it, before the better part of my character could intervene.

I am not asking you to pretend it did not happen. I am asking only for the justice that my tenderness deserves. You know my tenderness. You have known it since October, since the first letters, since the first morning I appeared at your door with nothing coherent to say and you let me in anyway. That tenderness is real and it does not change when I fail it in a moment of heat. It is not conditional on my being, at every moment, the best version of myself.

I am asking: in the name of everything you hold most dear, give me back what I have earned. Order whatever you want from me — any proof of my feeling, however demanding. I would do it with joy. I would do it with more than joy. I would do it with the whole of the relief of someone who has been lost and found the path again.

Say a word if you cannot yet believe me. I will always be ready to tell you the truth, even when the truth is embarrassing, even when it reveals a capacity for pettiness I wish I did not have.

I will not abandon you. Let me try, at least, to deserve you again.

Vienna, summer 1761.

I will be honest with you, my dear sister: I am not thinking about you very much today.

This is a lie, obviously. You can see through it from across the corridor. But I am trying on the posture of someone who has a devotional practice to protect and who intends, for once, to actually protect it rather than immediately composing long notes about the person who most distracts the devotional mood.

I do not think I am inconstant. Not in the way the word usually means. What I have with you is not a passing enthusiasm that burns bright and leaves ash. It is something else — something more structural, something that has become part of how I organize my days and interpret my experience and understand what I value. That is not inconstancy. That is, in fact, the opposite.

But I am not writing to you at great length today. I am not going to do it. I am going to say only: I have carried out your commissions, I take only tobacco and none of the other indulgences you probably assume, I am in a state of devotional enthusiasm which I would rather not disturb by too much self-analysis, and I love you, and I am coming back to you as soon as I return.

I kiss you and love you with my whole heart. The Archduke kisses you. I will kiss my sister Elisabeth on your behalf.

If you are still alive when I arrive — if the heat has not destroyed you, if the boredom of our separation has not proved fatal — I intend to see you immediately and continue this conversation in a more satisfying medium than ink.

Vienna, summer 1761.

Dear Laurette. I cannot help it — I have to ask how you slept.

You were so tired last night, after all the hours of it, after everything we did with the day, and I have been lying here in the morning wondering whether the fatigue broke properly in sleep or whether you turned in the dark the way I turned, restless with the residue of too much feeling.

Zerbin only dreams of his dear Laurette. I wrote that as a joke, as the conventional complaint of the comedy lover, but there is a thread of literal truth in it that I am choosing to acknowledge this morning, in this particular tone of early light, when the distance between the theatrical and the real seems thinner than usual. I did dream of you. My head was full of you — full of your face, your voice, the particular way you are when you are not performing for anyone.

I want you to know that I notice the difference. Between the public you and the one who exists in the hours when there is no audience. Both are real, both are you, but the second one — the one I have access to in moments that have no official status, that would not be recorded in any court diary — that one I hold in especial regard. That one I turn toward in my sleep without choosing to.

How is your head this morning? Is it well? Do you need anything? I have nothing necessary in front of me for the next two hours and am entirely at your disposal if you want company, or food, or someone to sit with you in comfortable silence, or someone to talk to — whatever form of presence would be most useful to you right now.

I am here. I am always here. Tell me how you slept.

Vienna, summer 1761.

The tarantula has bitten me and will not let me alone for a single moment.

I had promised to leave. I had every intention of honoring that promise — I had arranged myself to leave, mentally and physically, I had said my farewells to my own state of mind and prepared to re-enter the ordinary world with the dignity and composure of someone who has things in hand. And then the tarantula struck. The music. The idea. The particular direction the afternoon took once the idea got hold of me.

You know what the tarantula is. It is the thing that bites and does not release, the obsession that is also a joy, the compulsion that one does not regret even while acknowledging that it has thoroughly defeated any other plans. In Naples and in the Italian south, they say the tarantella was invented to cure the bite — that the only way to survive the poison is to dance it out, to move until the body has discharged what the bite put in.

I have been thinking about this. About us. About the possibility that what has happened to me since October is a version of being bitten, and that the only cure is to keep moving — to keep writing, to keep appearing at your door, to keep the correspondence and the visits and the music and the long conversations going until whatever the tarantula injected into me has found its way out of my system.

Though I suspect, honestly, that it will not. I suspect the cure is the disease in this case, and that I will be dancing it out for the rest of my life.

Does the three-hour meeting still hold? I will be there the moment I can manage it.

Vienna, summer 1761.

I am writing to you on the back of a note I was writing to someone else, and you will have no difficulty guessing to whom I was writing first. I am telling you this because there is something pleasing about that ordering — the other note, then yours, then perhaps another — this sequence in which you occupy the center of my correspondence in a way that no court protocol would sanction but which has become simply the shape of my days.

Someone I like better than anyone else gets my attention between obligations. That is the truth of it.

I am working on the second part of the essay. I hope to have it done before we leave for Holitsch, though my current state of mind is not conducive to the orderly development of philosophical argument. My current state of mind is, in fact, exactly what makes the philosophy difficult: I am trying to think about happiness and contentment and the interior life, and the interior life keeps interrupting the argument to present specific evidence that the argument has not yet accounted for.

The evidence is you. It is always you. You are both the subject and the obstacle, the thing I am trying to understand and the thing that makes understanding difficult by being so immediately, insistently present in my thoughts.

I know what caused my bad mood. I did not see you all evening yesterday. I walked in the garden and the garden was beautiful and entirely insufficient without your company. I am annoyed at myself for this transparency, for the degree to which my well-being has come to depend on such a specific and uncontrollable variable.

I would trade almost anything for the afternoon to hold us both.

Vienna, August 29, 1761, four o'clock in the afternoon.

Although it has not been long since you left, the time seems very long to me.

I am sitting at my writing table in the afternoon heat, which is still considerable, and I am aware of the particular quality of your absence, which is different from ordinary absence. You have been gone since this morning and the rooms have a different weight to them, as though something has shifted in the air pressure of the building, as though the Hofburg itself is responding to the fact of your not being in it.

I pity you the heat and the boredom of wherever you are. I pity myself, more selfishly, the interval.

After you left, I did something I had not entirely planned. I sat down with my thoughts — the ones your letter from yesterday provoked, the philosophical ones, the ones that had been forming since I read what you wrote about beauty and obligation and the nature of a life well lived — and I began to write them out. It became more than I expected. It became something like an essay, something I thought you might want to read, something that felt too good to keep to myself.

I showed it to the Empress. I should not have — or rather, I did so accidentally, because Madame d'Erdédy was there and in the flow of conversation it was handed over before I quite decided to hand it over. Now the Empress has it and has not yet returned it and I am waiting with the particular anxiety of someone who has shown an intimate thing to a person of power and cannot take it back.

If I get it back, you will have it. If not, I will write it again for you. Nothing I thought of was thought for her. It was thought for you.

Vienna, late summer-autumn 1761.

I promised you good weather today and the weather has not cooperated and I am sorry, though the fault is Boreas's and not mine, and I am registering my complaint with the relevant mythological parties.

The rain has changed everything. Music helps and then it does not. Society offers comfort and then falls short. I went hunting, which is a remedy that usually works for bad moods by requiring the full attention of the body and leaving no room for the mind's more troublesome activities, but even hunting has not entirely solved the problem today.

Here is the problem: when the light is bad and the weather turns and everything in the court takes on that slightly grey and obligatory quality that bad autumn weather produces, I miss you acutely. Not merely as a pleasantness I prefer — acutely, like a physical displacement, like standing in a room where something should be and finding it absent.

The most pleasant things lose their substance without you. This is inconvenient information about myself and I am sharing it with you anyway because I have given up filtering what I tell you.

But: there is something better coming. I have arranged — I will not explain the full diplomacy of it — that we will have the whole of the day after tomorrow together, while the Empress is at Colloredo's. The whole day. With no requirement to be anywhere or be anyone in particular. Just us, and whatever the day contains.

This is what I am holding against the grey weather.

Give me your orders and they will be carried out to the letter. In the meantime, I kiss you and embrace you, and I am counting the hours.

Vienna, autumn 1761.

I am very worried. I did not see you at the rosary and I need you to know that the worry is not purely spiritual.

I am twenty now. I said to myself, on the last day of the year, that at twenty one must be good, that twenty is the age at which one owes one's better nature the effort of being actually directed by it. I gave myself permission, in those last hours before the birthday, to be somewhat less than good — to be the person I am in the small hours, the one who sits in the dark with too much feeling and insufficient resolution — and told myself it was the last time. That today I begin the year in proper order.

And then I did not see you at the rosary, and the proper order was immediately insufficient, and I am writing to you from a place of considerable disorder.

The conversation I had with you yesterday — the talking that went on until something in my chest was physically worn out, until I had to drink barley water to restore myself, until I felt the particular depletion of someone who has spent too much of themselves in a direction they cannot stop spending — that conversation was everything I intended to leave behind when I turned twenty.

But I cannot.

I dare say you owe me this friendship, if only because of all the physical symptoms you have produced in me. My dried-out chest. My consumed evenings. My entirely reorganized understanding of what I want from this life, which turns out to be simpler and more specific than anything Parma prepared me for.

You. Primarily and continuously, you.

Vienna, early January 1762.

The Empress is better. Her headache has lifted since it — I will spare the details, which are both medical and undignified — and she slept for half an hour which did her considerable good, and when I came in she had a little heat but no alteration whatsoever, which is the best one can say of an empress in her present condition and which I am telling you because you will want to know it before anything else.

This is what we are, now. We are people who exchange information about the Empress's digestion at the end of an evening, by candlelight, in notes slipped under doors. We are people embedded in the deepest machinery of this family's health and governance and daily management of itself. I find I do not mind this. I find I am, in fact, grateful for it — not because I am devoted to the machinery (I am, but that is a separate thing) but because it is the infrastructure within which we exist, within which our correspondence has its occasion, its excuse, its cover.

I would write to you without the cover. I want to be clear about that. If there were no Empress, no illnesses, no diplomatic pretexts, no family news requiring transmission, I would still be writing to you in the evenings, with the same or greater urgency, about nothing that the world would call important.

But the Empress is there and she is better and that is genuinely good news and I wanted you to have it immediately.

Goodnight. I kiss you and kiss you with all the force I have left in me after this long evening, which is considerable.

Vienna, between January 15 and 17, 1762.

Brother Ferdinand slept uneasily from ten until midnight. He woke complaining a great deal. His stomach was rubbed with the medicine and then he slept for two more hours, peacefully this time. After that he asked to be taken out, which was a good sign, and the tension in his stomach has decreased and he is quite cheerful.

I am writing this to you because you are the one I write to when there is news that matters, good or bad, and this is news that matters, and you will understand precisely the mixture of relief and continued vigilance it contains.

We have been through this before. The weeks of watching Charles, which ended as they ended, are present in both our minds while we watch Ferdinand now, and there is a way in which the familiarity with this kind of vigil — the night-by-night monitoring, the careful report of symptoms, the fragile confidence that this night was better than the last — is almost a comfort. Almost. Because we know it is also fragile.

I am no less eager to tell you pleasant news than unpleasant. This is a thing I have learned about myself since October: I want you to have everything. The full report, the undoctored account, the real shape of what is happening. With you I am not curating.

Until tomorrow morning I cannot say anything with confidence. The night ahead will tell us more.

Farewell. Come to me if you can, or let me come to you. We should not be apart on nights like this. I sleep better when you are somewhere nearby, even if only in the adjacent wing, even if only accessible by letter.

Vienna, February 1762.

Hello, adorable sister. Good morning.

Until I can come to you in person — which I intend to do within the hour, as soon as I am dressed — I cannot resist writing to you first, because there are things I need to say to you that come easier in writing than in speech. You know which things. The ones that when we are in the same room together give way entirely to the desire to simply be near you, to abandon the argument and take the immediate thing instead.

My chest is still exhausted from yesterday. I told you things I have never told anyone, and told them at length, and the telling cost me physically — I am aware of it this morning in the particular tiredness of my throat, the way my voice feels used up. But not regretted. Not regretted at all.

You are the only person in my life to whom I can communicate things I cannot communicate to anyone else. I want you to hold that knowledge as carefully as I hold it. What passes between us is not general — it is specific to us, made of the particular overlap of how we think and what we have been honest with each other about, and I would not want it to exist in any other context.

When we see each other, the most beautiful ideas give way to the desire to kiss. I write this knowing that it might alarm you and writing it anyway, because you do not like excessive sweetness and I am trying to be honest rather than sweet. It is simply true. It is the most precise description of what happens to me when you are in the room.

I am coming to your house. Have the morning free if you can. I need to speak to you.

Vienna, 1762.

I had you this morning. I am writing those words and leaving them there, because they contain everything, because the morning was what it was and the afternoon is now the afternoon and I am in my rooms with the residue of it and I want to mark the day somehow.

Unless the Archduke sends an order — which he might; there is always the possibility — I will not call you back today. Not because I would not want to. But because I have myself to continue what you know, and because the order, if it came, would be its own kind of sweetness, its own kind of permission that the day has not otherwise offered.

This is how we live, you and I. In the gaps between the official schedule. In the hours that do not appear in any court diary, that cannot be accounted for publicly as anything other than the ordinary movements of women in a palace, unremarkable and unrecorded. We have built something real in those hours. I think of it often — the weight and texture of what we have built — and I find it extraordinary that it exists, that it has been allowed to exist, that the world has not yet found a way to close the gap through which it breathes.

I will not call you back unless he sends the order. But if he sends it — if the official architecture of the day creates, by accident or design, another gap — I want you to know that the call will be a willing one. That it will be made with all the feeling that this morning contained and more.

Goodnight, my sister. I kiss you for everything that may happen, a thousand times and a thousand times more, with all my heart.

Vienna, February 1762.

Madame d'Erdédy wants me to make very clear that my illness today consists entirely of having my fingers worn out from writing to you. This is her diagnosis. She delivered it with the expression of a woman who has seen a great deal and is choosing, diplomatically, to find it amusing.

I do nothing to correct her diagnosis because I don't want to distress you and because, also, it would take at least twenty notes to properly mend what needs mending if one is not sufficient to persuade you that I am well.

Here is what actually happened today: the little one danced against my stomach. By which I mean the child I carry — for I am carrying a child now, and the child has opinions about my movements, and today she expressed them by pressing and turning inside me until I had to lie down on the Empress's sofa and eat a piece of bread and breathe carefully until the dancing subsided. After that I went to the rosary. After the rosary I returned to my rooms and wrote to you.

I am dying of love for you. I am pregnant with a child who will be born in a few months. These two facts coexist in my body right now, in my rooms, in the winter afternoon, and I am trying to hold both of them with something like grace.

I am doing well. Better than well. If you disagree, get big yourself and gather the experience.

Farewell. I kiss you again. Madame d'Erdédy places herself at your feet and I place my whole heart there, with the absolute and permanent sincerity of someone who has nothing left to pretend.

Vienna, February 1762.

With donkeys, one must behave as with a Gene.

I wrote that and I am keeping it. It is what I mean. You behave exactly as you please and you know exactly what you are doing and I find it maddening and wonderful in approximately equal measure, and the only reasonable response is to repay you for your 'this can't be' with something in kind.

You said 'this can't be' and your face, when you said it, had the expression of someone who has decided to hold a position and is enjoying the holding of it far more than the position itself deserves. I noticed. I notice everything about your face, which is perhaps the most readable thing I have ever encountered — not in the sense that the court reads it, which they do not, not properly — but in the sense that I have spent long enough in its company to understand its grammar.

The grammar of your face, when you say 'this can't be': you are not certain it cannot be. You are considering the question while presenting the conclusion. There is a micro-interval of genuine uncertainty in there, before the decision closes.

I intend to find that interval and inhabit it.

So: behave as you please. You are the donkey and I am the Gene — the particular, stubborn, equal creature who is not fooled by the performance and who has the patience to wait out whatever theatrical certainty you choose to deploy against me.

I will repay you. With pleasure. Slowly and precisely and without any doubt at all about what I am doing.

Farewell, my dearest donkey. I love you with the full and irreversible commitment of someone who has considered the alternatives and found them entirely insufficient.

Vienna, February 1762.

Oh, my Gne — because I, too, am a donkey, and this particular pair of donkeys has apparently established a private language that I find more satisfying than the official ones I was raised in.

You want me to call you baadwaschl. You want me to write it down, to commit it to paper, to give it the permanence of ink. Very well. There it is. In Viennese slang: washcloth. My washcloth. My beloved, my sister, my dear and irreplaceable washcloth.

I am writing you a very short note today because that is what the donkey protocol apparently requires, even though I have the most beautiful things to say to you, things that have been accumulating since this morning and that require considerable space to be properly expressed. I am being obedient. I am being — and I want you to appreciate the effort this costs me — entirely obedient to your wishes, which is itself one of the most beautiful things I could say about us, that I am capable of this particular form of compliance with you when I am capable of it with very few others.

Baadwaschl. You want me to call you that because it gives you joy. And so I will, because your joy gives me joy, because the sight of your face in a moment of genuine pleasure is one of the primary goods of my present existence, because I am a donkey in love with another donkey and neither of us is pretending otherwise.

Farewell, my dear baadwaschl. I have the most beautiful things to say to you. They are waiting for when we are in the same room.

Vienna, February-March 1762.

Hello, my favorite donkey. My dearest Gne.

You do me an unspeakable harm by thinking I always forget everything. I do not always forget everything. I forget specific things — the furniture, for instance, which I left at your house not because I am careless but because leaving it there was a way of leaving a piece of myself in your space, which I am aware sounds more romantic than it is, but which is nonetheless the truth of what I was doing. I am not careless with you. I am strategically present.

You would have been right to reproach me on Saturday. Today you are wrong. Note the distinction. I am keeping careful track of which days I am in the right and which I am not, and today is mine.

I am overjoyed that you are well again. Truly overjoyed — not in the polished court sense of the word but in the actual sense, the interior sense, the sense in which overjoyed means something happened to my body when I heard the news, something that could be called relief but is larger than relief and more personal. The days when you are unwell are days that have a different quality than other days. Everything functions less well. I move through them with a particular carefulness, as though the world has become temporarily fragile.

Here are two languages for you — Italian and Spanish, what I have assembled for your amusement. Me ne rallegro assai: I rejoice greatly. Y deseo que continu tambien: and I desire that this continues as well. Joy and its continuation. That is the whole prayer.

I am dying of love for you. I want to tell you this again, again, for as many times as there are pages left. I love you.

Summer 1763. Because you were very good and slept well, I am sending you your table. This is the logic of our arrangement: good behavior rewarded, in this case with the table I have been making for you, which is not entirely finished but enough finished to send.

I am feeling pretty good today. This is worth recording because the bar has been variable and I want you to have an accurate account for comparison. Pretty good means: my head is clear, my chest is manageable, the thing I was afraid might happen has not yet happened, and I am standing at the window looking at Vienna in summer and feeling something very close to uncomplicated contentment.

We had a small earthquake last night. Between two and three in the morning — a brief trembling, the kind that wakes you unsure whether it was real or dreamed, and then a violent wind that rose after it. I lay awake watching the dawn appear in weather that made me shudder. There is a particular horror to a frightening sunrise, to the way it offers the usual promise of morning and withdraws it immediately.

But then the day continued, and here we are, and I am leaving for Hetzendorf, and I want you to look out the window as I pass. A glance through the window is not nothing. 1763. I saw you at the rosary yesterday and had not yet read your note. I read it afterward with more attention than I had given it at first, because something in your face when you saw me at the rosary suggested the note contained more than the usual news.

October-November, 1763. You are too good to send me food after everything I have done to deserve your frustration. I know this. I sat with the delivery for a long time before I could bring myself to open it, because opening it would require acknowledging the full weight of your generosity toward someone who had spent the morning being ungrateful.

I love you adoringly. This is the sentence I want you to read first, before the qualifications and the reflections and the various observations about our situation that I am about to make. My happiness is to love you, and to be loved by you. It is the greatest contentment I can have.

You also know that I constantly pursue you. I do it because I love you. Your perfection is all I wish for — I want you to be well, to be wise, to be happy in ways that do not require my presence, and also I want your presence at all times, which is a contradiction I have stopped trying to resolve.

Perhaps we will be separated. Perhaps we will no longer be together in the easy way we have been together. These moments were too sweet for me to be able to pretend they will simply continue — I know how precarious beauty is, how quickly the court arranges and rearranges the circumstances of people's lives. What I can tell you is that whatever comes, my life is dear to me only because it is dedicated to you.

I am perhaps an object of sin to you — a small one, I flatter myself. I ask your forgiveness for everything I might have written and for everything I have felt without permission.

October-November, 1763. Good morning, dear — I need a better word for you than the ones available, but I will start with this. I have already played the violin. I have been neither eating nor writing nor painting, and the only resource left to me is this: presenting myself at your feet in writing, being too lazy or too afraid to do it in reality.

I had wanted to come to you in person this morning. You wanted to know my news. Here it is: my head, my chest, my stomach are doing wonderfully, all of them, and I am very worried about Marie-Anne's cold, and I have a presentiment that I cannot explain and cannot shake.

For two days now I have been held by a certainty that this year will be my last. I know how this sounds. I know you will scold me for it and call it morbidity and tell me to eat properly and sleep and stop composing my own ending before it has been written. But I want to tell you, because I tell you everything that matters: the presentiment does not frighten me. It spreads a sweetness through me, a kind of interior peace that I have not found in philosophy or prayer, and that seems — this is the part that will most alarm you — to come from certainty rather than despair.

I am not a saint. My head is quite possibly spinning. The person most likely to go mad in this family is me, and I am aware of this, and I want it noted.

But I wanted you to know. I wanted you, of all people, to know how it feels from the inside.

October-November, 1763. It is in the midst of misery that I write to you. Not the misery of catastrophe — nothing so dramatic — but the low, persistent misery of a day that has refused to arrange itself into any form of happiness.

The Archduke no longer goes out on horseback. This is the news. I say it as baldly as I felt it, which is to say: flatly, with the particular resignation of a woman who has been managing inconveniences for long enough that one more lands differently than it once would have. We cannot be happy in every way. This is a truth I have known for years and that I keep discovering, as though its freshness were somehow renewable.

I am writing to you because I am in the midst of misery and you are the person I write to from the midst of things. This is one of the central facts of our relationship — that I do not save myself up for you, do not present only the polished and managed version, do not appear in your correspondence only when I have something beautiful to say. I appear when I am in the midst of things and need to be somewhere that is not inside my own head.

You receive this with such steadiness. You receive all of it — the beauty and the misery and the midpoints — and you write back, and something in the act of writing back constitutes a kind of grace that nothing else in my life provides.

The Archduke does not ride. The day is hard. I am with you in writing. That will have to be sufficient today.

October-November, 1763. I cannot speak to you and I could not even if I wanted to, and so I write. This is the particular mercy of letters: when speech fails or is forbidden — when the room is too full, when voices carry, when the whole architecture of this life makes the direct route impossible — there is always the page.

I kiss you a thousand and a thousand times with all my heart. I need to say this before anything else, before the court news and the health reports and the management of arrangements — I kiss you with everything I have, which is considerable, which has always been the problem and the gift.

Something is changing. I feel it in the way one feels changes in weather before they arrive, the particular pressure shift. I do not want to name it. I am not ready to name it. November, 1763. I would like to write you something beautiful but I cannot think of what beautiful would look like from inside this month. November has its particular quality and this November is darker than most, and the beautiful things I want to say to you all have a black border around them.

So instead I will tell you plainly: Archduchess Isabeau is going to die soon. She tells you this finally, because the illness will get worse, and the disease is all the more dangerous because the only means there could be cannot be used. You know what I mean. The means — being with you, the specific relief of proximity to you — is precisely what the illness now makes unavailable.

She is dying of love for you. She knows this sounds like a figure of speech and she means it as direct reporting. The illness and the love are not separate things. The love is the thing that makes the illness matter, that makes any particular day matter — because you are in it, because I am oriented toward you, because being alive is meaningful in direct proportion to your presence in the meaning.

She should still love you. She cannot stop. I think it would be best to tell you soon — when I see you, which I intend to be soon, I will say it all in person and then I will be well again. The face is a little sick. Your favorite place is not.

November, 1763. Do not think I write to arrange an appointment. On the contrary, I am asking you not to come after the rosary tonight. This is not a farewell — not yet, not in the way that word has been hovering at the edges of my thoughts. It is only: I need to write this down, and I need you to read it, and I need the privacy that comes from words on a page rather than breath in a room.

I have been thinking about what I will leave you with. Not possessions — though the table is yours, the paintings will be divided as they should be — but the accumulated meaning of everything I have wanted to tell you and kept finding the wrong moment to say. Today I am making this the right moment.

I start from a heart full of your image. As long as I have lived I have tried to lead you along a clear path, and as long as I could do it without revealing too much of myself, I stayed silent. I am less silent now.

Your duty was to speak before loving — that is what I would say to you if I were advising someone else about what you have done. You loved before you knew if it was permitted. You wrote before you could be certain it was safe. You were, perhaps, seduced by imprudence. So was I.

The Empress will be kind to you after I am gone. She sees me in you. Hold that. Never abandon frankness, even when prudence counsels otherwise. Your sincerity is your best quality and also your most dangerous one: guard it as such.

I adore you. This is the beginning and the end of all of it. I adore you, and this life has been dear to me only because it was lived toward you.
